note: Every claim this archive has published and then had to take back, with what was said, what is true, and how the mistake was made. It is kept because an archive that only shows its successes is not telling you how reliable it is. Corrections are made **in the place where the mistake was made**, not quietly on a back page — this list is the index to them.
lead: Twenty things this archive got wrong.

rows.what: A panel said «not tracked per volume» over rows whose own marks said «never opened».
rows.where: /map/ — the coverage timeline in the marker panel
rows.said: Gračišće's **Births** heading read *«10 volumes · 1 read, 0 part read, 9 unopened»* and its **Marriages** heading, two lines below, read *«8 volumes · not tracked per volume»* — while the mark beside every one of those eight marriage volumes was the open circle for **never opened**.
rows.true:
**Tracking is a property of the place, not of one record type in it.** The heading asked whether any volume *of that kind* carried a read flag; the marks have always asked the question of the parish. So a parish where one baptism book is recorded as read announced that its marriages were untracked, and then marked them as checked negatives in the same panel.

**They ask the same question now.** If this archive keeps a per-volume record for a parish at all, a volume with no flag **has not been opened**, and the heading says so: Gračišće's marriages read *«none read, 8 never opened»*. Where the archive tracks nothing at a place — Žminj, and most of the map — it still says **not tracked per volume**, because that is a different and weaker thing and the distinction is the whole point of having four marks instead of three.
rows.how: David: «why are we not «tracking per volume» e.g in the attached for marriages?»

rows.what: Ninety-four people whose only source is the family tree were wearing the strongest provenance band on the page.
rows.where: /who/ — the band under every name in the family figure
rows.said: Every box in the family figure carries a band saying how the person is known: **the archive's own line · a register read here · a FamilySearch index entry · the family tree, unverified**. The rule that chose it read *«if this row is flagged as the compiler's kin, say «the archive's own line»»* — **and checked that before it checked where the fact came from.**
rows.true:
**`mine` is a statement about kinship and it was being printed where the reader looks for provenance.** Ninety-four rows carry both that flag and a MyHeritage identifier, and every one of them was claiming the strongest band on the page — including **every person the Australian and Crikvenica branches brought in on 15 and 16 September**, whose only source is David's family tree.

**The evidence wins now.** The drawn descent keeps «the archive's own line»; a row read off a register page — the Gologorica and Gračišće work — says **a register read here**, which twelve of them were not getting either; an ark says **index**; a tree identifier says **the family tree, unverified**; and kinship with no other source falls through to «line» last.

**Thirty-two people now read as tree-sourced and fifteen as register-read**, where before both were hidden inside twenty-four «own line».
rows.how: David, looking at Antony De Franceski's page: *«petrica was a woman and has children, you arent reading myheritage gedcom?»* She **is** in the archive — her page draws her husband and both daughters — but on her brother's page she was a bare name in a box, and the box was claiming a provenance she does not have. **A sibling box now says when that person heads a household of their own**, so a sister with two daughters stops looking like the end of a line.

rows.what: Layering three maps put three legends on one picture, and two of their colours were the same colour.
rows.said: The three maps were merged with their own palettes carried over intact, and for a day that was harmless because only one legend showed at a time. **Layering them broke it in the same stroke that made them useful.**
rows.true:
Measured in CIELAB, **eight pairs of colours across the three legends were closer than ΔE 20** — the point at which two dots stop being reliably tellable apart — and two pairs were effectively one colour:

· **«Every volume read» and «Both, at one place» were the same hex value**, ΔE 0.0.
· **«Researched, books unopened» and «Where they went»** were ΔE 1.7 apart.
· «Istria, where the name is» sat 12 from one and 19 from another.

**Re-cut as three families that cannot be confused for one another**: the shelf is a warm ramp — **red for catalogued and never opened**, orange for researched, amber for a volume read, green for finished, grey for not in any catalogue; our people are **violet through pink**; the ground is **blue**. No pair is now closer than ΔE 21, and the only pairs near that are inside the people family, which is one question's sub-categories.

**And hue is not the only channel any more.** A marker's ring says which layer it is being coloured from — thin white for the shelf, deep violet for our people, navy for the ground — because a reader looking at one dot should not have to work out which of three legends it belongs to.

**Red also does work the old sand did not.** Twelve hundred of the 1,235 shelf places are catalogued and never opened, and the map now looks like that.
rows.how: David, on Pićan: *«it looks like the colour is «every volume read» or is the colour «researched, books unopened»? colours are way too close to one another. if not opened it should be red».* Pićan was «researched, books unopened» and sat beside a gold marker it could not be told from.

rows.what: Antony De Franceski was published as «Zdravko and Ruža's only child» on a day this archive had already found his sister.
rows.said: The page opened: *«**Anton Mario De Franceski**, born **21 August 1944 at Reutlingen** — Zdravko and Ruža's **only child**, and the four-year-old who sailed with them.»* Below it, in the same column, the archive printed **«No family is drawn for this name, and no record stands behind it»** — under four sentences naming his parents, his father's date of birth and the file they are all three on.
rows.true:
**He had a sister, and this archive found her the same afternoon it wrote «only child».** **Petrica Defranceski** was born at Horsham nine years after the family landed, and she is the reason the whole Australian branch came into the archive at all — David asked why she was not here.

**The second sentence was worse than wrong, it was structural.** `households.json` is built from registers, and this family's modern generations have never been in a register this archive can reach, so **the mini-tree had nothing to draw from** — for Antony, for Zdravko, for David's own father, for David. Nine households have been added from the family's own tree and the documents already held, marked as tree-derived and not register-read. Antony's page now draws his parents, his sister, his wife and his two children.

**And thirty internal links across the person pages were printing as literal square brackets** — including the one on this page — because the renderer that page keeps has never understood a link. It does now.
rows.how: David: *«this doesnt make sense. if he is Zdravko's son then you should be able to draw this tree? along with his sister, and kids».* Both faults were visible on one screen and neither had been noticed by the archive that wrote them.

rows.what: Fourteen people were counted as the compiler's own kin on the strength of a shared surname on a headstone.
rows.where: /people/ — the «★ My line» filter · /who/ · the map
rows.said: **199 roster rows carried the `mine` flag**, which drives the *«★ My line»* filter on [the people page](/people/) and decides who is counted as this family rather than as somebody else of the name. **Nothing ever tested it.** Two of the 199 were Mario Defranceschi of Brisbane, corrected earlier today.
rows.true:
**A test, written down for the first time: «mine» means this archive can NAME the path from this person to David** — a place on the direct line, a named relationship, or a household the archive has actually drawn. A shared surname on a gravestone is not a path.

Twelve more rows fail it, and they are all Find a Grave memorials with no join to anything: **Joachim Bruno and Gerda at Millbrook, Conchita in the Bronx, Joseph and Basilio at East Farmingdale, John A. and Bruno at Middle Village, Edward «Dado» at Hartsdale** — the American wave — and **Adelia at Lilydale, Corrado at Fawkner and Attilio at Parkville**, which the diaspora page had *already* filed under the **Italian post-war assisted migration**, and which it says in as many words is not the same movement as this family's.

The flag comes off all twelve. They stay in the archive, where they belong; they are no longer counted as kin. **185 rows keep it**, every one of them either on the direct line, carrying a named relationship, or standing in a household this archive has drawn.
rows.how: Written into the work list this evening as a consequence of the Mario error, and run the same night rather than left.

rows.what: The roster is still built on the July 2018 GEDCOM. The live tree has nearly twice as many people in it, and a whole Australian branch this archive had never heard of.
rows.where: everywhere the roster is read — /who/, /people/, the map, the atlas
rows.said: The archive cites **«MyHeritage family tree export, July 2018 — a GEDCOM of 8,286 individuals, 254 of them carrying this surname»** as its family-file source, and 513 roster rows carry an identifier from it. A reconciliation note of **7 September 2026** already recorded that *«the 2018 GEDCOM is superseded and must not be used again»* — the live tree holds **15,643** people — and read 459 individuals of the surname out of the live tree. **That reading was never imported.** The roster was left as it was.
rows.true:
**David found it by looking at his own tree**: *«Anton has a sister in Horsham. My heritage tree has all that info. Why don't you?»*

Because the roster had never been rebuilt from the live tree. Read out of it on 15 September, tree 4:

· **Petrica Defranceski**, Zdravko and Ruža's daughter — **the first of this line born in Australia**, at Horsham — and her husband Michael Baviello, their daughters Antonia and Carla, and two grandchildren.

· **Anton's own household**: his wife Marion Bain, his son Dean, and his daughter **Lisa, 1968–2015, born at Adelaide** — whom no search of this surname would ever have found, because the tree spells her *Defraneski*, missing the *c*.

· **Zdravko's three other siblings**, all born at Crikvenica: **Josip Petar «Pepo» 1911–1980**, who never left; **Petar Vid «Pero» 1913**, the *Petar* of the Pfullingen file, died in Germany; and **Anka Nera, 1915–1944, dead at Belgrade aged twenty-nine** — about whom this archive knows nothing at all.

Fifteen people added. **The whole live tree still has to be reconciled**, and this is one branch of it.
rows.how: David, looking at the tree on his phone. The archive had the 2018 file's people and had mistaken that for having the family.

rows.what: Mario Defranceschi of Brisbane was flagged as this family. He is a placeholder in the tree, and I repeated the error to David in conversation.
rows.said: Two roster rows — **«Mario De Franceschi, 15 Sep 1938 – 29 Jan 2013»** off a Find a Grave memorial at Centenary Memorial Gardens, and **«Mario Defranceschi, 1938–2013»** out of MyHeritage — were both flagged **`mine`**, this archive's marker for the compiler's own family. Brisbane's marker on the map showed him and nobody else. **Asked why his own household was not there, I told David the map was showing «your father Mario». It was not.**
rows.true:
**David's father is Ivan Anton Defranceski, 1951–2026**, generation 7 of the direct line: Senj → Johannesburg → Brisbane. The direct line has no Mario in it anywhere.

In David's live tree, **Mario Defranceschi 1938–2013's parents are «QLD Defranceschi (Deceased)» and «Unknown Defranceschi»** — placeholder nodes, a stub for an unconnected Queensland family of the name. And [the diaspora page](/diaspora/) had already filed *«Mario at Brisbane, 1938–2013»* with the **Italian post-war assisted migration** of the 1950s and 60s, which it says in as many words is *not the same movement* as the Croatian displaced persons of 1949.

The flag is removed and he is filed under *other families of the name*. **Two errors, and the second is mine**: the archive mis-flagged him, and I read the flag off the screen and told David it was his father rather than checking the direct line, which was one file away.
rows.how: Found while pulling the Australian branch out of the live tree, by asking who Mario's parents were.

rows.what: «He was nine years old» on the ship. He was four.
rows.said: Explaining why Anton stood first of the three consecutive numbers on the *General M B Stewart* manifest, this archive wrote: *«Anton first because the list is alphabetical by forename inside the surname, and **he was nine years old**.»*
rows.true:
**He was four.** Anton was born at Reutlingen on **21 August 1944** — on the Reutlingen residence list, on the Neuhausen list, on IRO card 52852, and now on **NAA A11534, 58–60**, an Australian file of 1948 that names all three of them with dates of birth. The ship sailed from Naples on 17 March 1949. He was four years and seven months old.

The reason for the order was right; the age attached to it was invented.
rows.how: Found while answering David's question about Antony De Franceski of Willowbank, by searching the National Archives of Australia — which turned out to hold the household's dates of birth in one line.

rows.what: Zdravko is buried once at Horsham, not twice. «Zorafko» is the same man.
rows.said: The graves list carried **two** Horsham memorials: *«Zdravko «Frank» Defranceski, 1921 – 22 Dec 1979»* and *«Zorafko Frank De Franceski, – 27 Dec 1979, CENTRAL 2-J-10»*. They were counted as two people.
rows.true: **One man, one grave, two memorials.** «Zorafko» is how Australian officialdom wrote him from the day he landed: **NAA B78, YUGOSLAVIAN/DEFRANCESKI ZORAFKO — «Arrived Melbourne per General M B Stewart 13 April 1949»**, the same voyage, the same household. A fourth spelling, *Zdrafko*, appears on his alien registration, **NAA A2571, number 76418**. The two dates are the death and the burial: he died on 22 December 1979 and was buried on the 27th.
rows.how: Found in the same NAA search. The archive had already noticed the two memorials and had not been able to say which was which.

rows.what: Twenty places on the research map were coloured «something here read» when not one of their register volumes had ever been opened.
rows.where: /map/ · the marker colours and the panel
rows.said: The map carried four colours and the third was **«Something here read»** — gold. Twenty-two markers were gold. The page said the scale meant **«how far we have got»** with the shelf, and the panel on a gold marker said *«Something here has been read — the search register says what. This archive does not yet track WHICH of these volumes.»* Read together, that says: we have opened books here and not written down which ones.
rows.true:
**Twenty of the twenty-two had never had a single register volume opened.** They were gold because the search register NAMES them — and what it names them for is *literature*. Žminj is the clean example: the two rows that flag it are **«Libri žminjski, libar drugi» (Žminj 2008)**, a local history sent by David, and **Darovec's 2021 migration paper**, which lists Žminj among the towns the Carni settled at. Both were read. Neither is a register.

Only **Mione (15 volumes)** and **Ovaro (1)** had a book of their own opened, and both are Antenati, the one provider whose catalogue carries a per-volume flag.

**Reading a book about a parish and reading the parish's own registers are two different acts**, and a scale whose legend says «how far we have got with the shelf» must not paint the first in the colour of the second. The two are now separate colours: **teal — researched, its own books unopened**, and **gold — a volume of its own registers read**. The map loses twenty gold markers and gains a state it did not have a word for.
rows.how: Found by David, looking at Žminj: «it's on the map as *something here read* but then none of the volumes are marked as *part read* or *read*». The per-volume marks added an hour earlier are what made the contradiction visible — the place said one thing and every book under it said another.

rows.what: I said Dubrovnik was too thin to be a group. It is a household.
rows.where: /dubrovnik/ · and a reply given on 13 September
rows.said: Asked whether the Rijeka, Dubrovnik and Bakar groups could each have a page, this archive answered that **Dubrovnik could not**: *«it's four people, and the 1829 row has four names in a parent list, which is exactly the tabular-register trap that burned us on Francisca. Giving it a page would dress four records as a group.»*
rows.true:
**The caution was right and the conclusion was wrong.** The trap was real. The answer was to *apply the rule*, not to walk away from the records.

Applied, the four resolve into one household across forty-two years. The 1829 row is a **marriage**, not a birth: four parent names is the signature of the Austrian tabular register, whose columns run SPONSI, SPONSAE, GENITORES SPONSI, GENITORES SPONSAE. Read that way it says **Matteo Persich, born 1829, son of Antonio Persich and Teresa Martecchini, marrying a daughter of Pietro Defranceschi** — and the other three records are that couple's children, baptised at Dubrovnik in 1853, 1863 and 1871.

**The children confirm the reading.** The first son is **Antonio**, his father's father. The daughter of 23 December 1863 is **Cattarina *Teresa* Vittoria Maria**, his father's mother. That is the ordinary Adriatic naming order, and it is independent of the row that was misread.

The lesson is not about Dubrovnik. **A rule this archive learned in order to avoid a false positive was used instead to avoid looking** — which costs more than the error it was guarding against.

And two smaller things fell out of it: the surname is **Martecchini**, not Martechini — forebears finds exactly one person of the archive's spelling in the world — and it is **Ragusan**, not Venetian, which is where this site had filed it on the strength of how it looks.

rows.what: The Search Register has been hiding forty-three per cent of itself
rows.said: That the Search Register listed every source this archive had examined — *«197 sources examined»*, as its own header said.
rows.true:
**It was showing 112 of them.** Eighty-five rows were on the page's data file and not on the page.

The cause is dull and the consequence is not. The template grouped rows by an `outcome` field and knew five values — *yield, partial, nothing, blocked, pending*. Over a year the rows had been written with twelve: **70 of them say «hit»**, seven say «miss», and the rest are «found», «note», «mixed», «correction», «clean». **Anything the template did not recognise was silently dropped.** No error, no gap, no warning — the row simply was not drawn.

So the register understated the work by a factor approaching two, and did it in the one place on this site whose entire purpose is to say honestly how much has been looked at. **A page that exists to record negative results was itself losing results.**

**And three of the eighty-five were written today, by me.** The Hungaricana searches and the ANNO search were all filed as «found», published, and were never visible. I found them missing only because I went back to check that a published finding had actually appeared — which is a habit this archive should make routine rather than occasional.

Fixed two ways: the twelve words are now mapped onto the five outcomes, and **any value that still is not recognised falls into an «Other» group rather than disappearing.** It is no longer possible for a row to be invisible. 197 render.

rows.what: I gave the harbour master's daughter the wrong allowance, off the line above
rows.said: That **Francziska Defranceschi**, the port captain's orphan daughter, drew a *kegydíj* of **80 forints** a year in the Hungarian state accounts of 1888 onward.
rows.true:
**Sixty-five.** The 1888 account reads, in order: *«2. Marussig Gentilének, Marussig Ferencz volt fiumei révkapitány árva leányának … évi **80** frt kegydij adományoztatott. 3. Defranceschi Francziska, Defranceschi Ferencz révkapitány árva leánya … évi **65** frt kegydijban részesült.»* The eighty belongs to the woman on the line above.

This is the same mistake this archive has made before and warned itself about: **reading the adjacent line**. It caught the Vodnjan mother out of an index list and the Zadar parents off a tabular marriage row, and it has now done it in a printed Hungarian budget where the two entries are numbered 2 and 3 and sit one under the other. The lesson does not get learned once.

The error was found the same day by going back to read the whole page rather than the search snippet — which is also the only thing that ever finds it.

**And the re-read gave two things the snippet had not.** The 1894 account styles him ***m. kir.* révkapitány** — *magyar királyi*, Royal Hungarian — the exact counterpart of the *Regii* written beside the name at Bakar in 1849. And the 1898 account says why Francziska was on the list at all: *«tekintettel vagyontalanságára, munka- és keresetképtelenségére»*, in view of her destitution and her incapacity for work or earning.

rows.what: The households list counts one Omiš family twice
rows.said: That this archive held **112 reconstructed households**, among them *Francesco Franceschi × Maria De Caralipco* at **Omiš**, 1854–1877, seventeen children, and *Francesco Franceschi × Maria De Caralipeo* at **Almissa**, 1856–1873, seven children — as two separate families.
rows.true:
**They are one family.** Almissa is simply the Italian name for Omiš, and the two mothers' surnames differ by a single letter that two indexers read differently. Six of the seven children in the smaller household are the *same named individuals* as in the larger one.

The error was mine and it was structural: the household builder keys on the place string as the index writes it, so a town recorded in two languages becomes two towns, and a wife spelled two ways becomes two wives. Nothing was invented — but a family was doubled, and the archive's household count is one too high.

**It is not only a subtraction.** The seventh child, **Carlo Paolo Michele Maria Franceschi**, appears in the smaller household and not in the larger. Merging them does not take a family away; it gives this one an eighteenth child. The duplicate is now flagged in the data and named on the page; the merge itself is held back because the household ids are referenced in several places and a silent renumbering would be worse than the duplicate.

rows.what: I corrected a note that was right
rows.said: That the working notes' line — *«**55 suppressed charts** to review by hand»* — was stale and wrong, and that the true figure was **763 of 1,056 dossiers with no pedigree chart**: *«wrong by a factor of fourteen, in the direction that makes the job look nearly done»*.
rows.true:
**The note was right and I was measuring something else.** A dossier has three possible states, not two:

**238** have a chart drawn. **55** have candidate households that the **date gate rejected every one of** — a chart *suppressed*, which is exactly what the note said and exactly the pile that needs reviewing by hand. **763** have **no household link at all**, so there is nothing to suppress and nothing to draw.

55 is the review queue. 763 is not a backlog; it is the shape of the evidence.
rows.how:
`v.get("ptree")` was read as «has a chart». It is not: the builder returns a `ptree` object carrying **`none: True`** when it found candidates and the gate threw them all out. Conflating «suppressed» with «absent» turned a precise note into a false alarm — and the alarm was published in a commit that was itself about numbers going stale.

The audit now prints all three states separately. **Being loudly right about an error is not the same as being right**, and the check I built to stop numbers rotting produced a rotten number on its first day.

rows.what: Twenty-four households with the parents the wrong way round
rows.said: Twenty-four of this archive's 112 households named a **De Franceschi woman as the father** and **her husband as the mother**. *«father: Michiela De Franceschi · mother: Domenico Giachin»*. Forty people's roster entries said things like *«**Domenico Giachin** — named as **mother** on 2 baptisms»*.
rows.true: Every one is inverted. The women are the mothers; the men are the fathers. **All 24 are De Franceschi daughters married out** — which is why the error clusters exactly where it does.
rows.how:
The households built from the FamilySearch index take the two parent names the index returns and assign them **by position**, not by sex. Where the De Franceschi parent was listed first — which is what happens when the *mother* is the one carrying this archive's surname — the pair went in backwards.

**So the bug bit precisely the people this archive is worst at tracking.** The whole Vodnjan argument is that «the surname keeps its sons and loses its daughters»; twenty-four married-out daughters were in the data and the data had them down as men.

Found while testing something else entirely — chasing whether one **Michiela De Franceschi fu Giuseppe** was a daughter of the Giuseppe this archive already documents. The check that found it is now in `scripts/audit.py` and runs on every publish: **a female given name in the father field**. It would have caught this the day it was introduced.

rows.what: Counted four candidates and could name three
rows.said: That **four** look-alike candidates had been examined at full magnification and given up on this film — *«q.m Francesco»*, *«di Francesco»*, *«da Francesche»*, «and one more».
rows.true: There are **three**. *«Nicolò Sussani q.m Francesco»* and *«Antonia Palin di Francesco»* on image 560, and *«Bonetta da Francesche»* at page 164, entry 21. There is no fourth.
rows.how:
A running tally kept in the head rather than in the file. The sentence was written, the fourth could not be named, and it went out anyway with «and one more» standing in for evidence.

Small, and caught within the minute — but it is the same shape as the mistake that put **1,952** on this site: **a number written before it was counted**. The count of things given up is exactly as much a claim as the count of things found, and this archive's whole argument is that it keeps both.

rows.what: Full-text result counts that were a year, not a count
rows.said: That FamilySearch's full-text search returned **1,952 results for *Gologorica*, 1,719 for *Gračišće* and 1,885 for *Defranceschi*** — and, noting how implausibly alike those three numbers were, that they «**have not been tested**» and should not be trusted.
rows.true:
Every one of the three is wrong, and the real figures are not close.

**Gologorica returns 19.** *Gračišće* three pages. *Crikvenica* fifteen. *Ližnjan* **two**. **Defranceschi returns about 9,900** — **five times** what was published, not a fifth of it. And **Vodnjan returns nothing at all**: the Croatian name post-dates every record in the corpus, which uses **Dignano** — about 12,200 of those, most of them the *other* Dignano, in Friuli.
rows.how:
The number was scraped with a loose pattern — `([0-9,]+)\s*Results` — off a page whose visible text ends *«… Border Crossing Records 1924-**1952**\nResults per page:»*. **It matched a year out of a collection title.** «1,952 results» was a border-crossing collection's end date standing next to the words «Results per page».

What makes this worse than a scraping bug: **the page said the numbers looked wrong and published them anyway.** Three unrelated searches returning numbers of the same size was called «the shape of a number that counts something other than what you think» — and then the one check that would have settled it, *look at how many results are actually on the page*, was not run. It takes one request.

**Flagging a doubt is not the same as resolving it.** A figure you have publicly called untrustworthy should not be in the sentence at all.

The finding underneath is unharmed and is better than it looked: **19 hits for Gologorica is a set small enough to read end to end**, which is exactly what makes the village sweep worth doing.

rows.what: A correction that never reached the data file
rows.said: The families page described the southern-Istrian family as «**Southern Istria — Pula, Fažana, Ližnjan**», resting on the name being «**in the Pula registers from 1667**».
rows.true: Those entries are from the **Svetvinčenat** register, DGS 005497884, and the parish carries the surname from **1657**. Pula holds ten register entries of the name, only three accepted, and four of them are spelt **Bellulovich Francessich** — a different surname.
rows.how: The correction itself was made days ago and published **on the lines chart**. It never reached `families.json`, which went on asserting the original claim in its own title. **This is the second time in this archive that a published correction has failed to reach the data behind it** — the first cost forty-four people their parish. Found by auditing the chart's place labels against every place string in the register, the roster and the households, which is a check that should run on a schedule and does not.

rows.what: Numbers I gave David before checking them
rows.said: That **Pula** had «about fifty records» and that **Krk, Kastav and Oprtalj** were towns missing from the lines chart.
rows.true: Pula has **ten** in the register. The fifty came from adding register, roster and households together and folding «Pola» into «Pula» — three different kinds of row counted as one kind. And Krk, Kastav and Oprtalj are **not gaps at all**: the surnames there are **Franceschini** and **Francetich**, different stocks of a different name.
rows.how: Caught before publishing, by recounting per source and printing the **spelling column** beside each place. The lesson is the one this archive keeps meeting from a new direction: **a place count means nothing until you have looked at what surname is actually standing in it.**

rows.what: A filter of mine deleted a paragraph of hers
rows.said: Nothing — that is the problem. The account of **Paputchka's death**, some five hundred words, **silently vanished from the transcription**.
rows.true: The scanner destroyed its opening sentence, returning *«WS CAPES FUG PS PEPE AU SII Pony FRU. OI WC PI PO UT UU TET»* where she had written *«We experienced "true" love with our Siberian Husky Paputchka»*. A rule I wrote to strip scanner noise matched that line — and because prose is stored **one line per paragraph**, deleting the line deleted **the entire paragraph**.
rows.how:
Restored word for word from the original, supplied by David, and **marked on the page** as restored so no reader has to wonder which text they are looking at.

The lesson is specific and unpleasant: **a cleanup rule that operates on a whole paragraph can destroy a whole paragraph.** Noise-stripping must be scoped to the noise — a few tokens — and never to the container it sits in. It was also **found by the reader, not by me**: nothing in the build warned that five hundred words had gone, because nothing was counting.

**A reconciliation was then run over the whole page** — every substantial line of the raw scan tested against the published text — and it found **four more losses of the same kind**: the closing paragraph of the husky piece, which had been left beginning mid-sentence at *«anger and rage»*; a sentence from *A Suicide Avenged*; a line of dialogue from it; and part of the godparents letter. All four are restored and marked. **One passage is unrecoverable** — three lines describing a person, from the 2004 course — and stands on the page as a stated gap rather than a silent one.

rows.what: A living man named in an allegation
rows.said: Her own introduction to the first poem was published word for word, and it **named the man she was then married to** in a sentence describing *«a long standing affair, committing adultery for years»*.
rows.true: **That should never have gone up.** It is an allegation of adultery against a **named living person**, published by this archive. That the words are hers and that she published them herself does not transfer the risk or the discretion — the archive chose to reproduce them.
rows.how:
The name is removed; the sentence now reads *«my marriage was over»*. It is **the single alteration to her text anywhere on that page**, and the page says so.

The failure was not ignorance of the rule. **The same rule had been applied an hour earlier**, and correctly, to a different document — a statement of allegations that was excluded entirely for naming living people. Then a transcription was published verbatim without running the same test over it. **A rule applied once is not a rule; it has to be run against every page that goes out.**

rows.what: «Corsica — not ours»
rows.said: The lines page filed Corsica under «**not ours**».
rows.true: **Nobody had checked.** Not one search had ever been run in a French archive for this surname, in any commune. «Not ours» was a **guess wearing the clothes of a finding** — the same error as a false join, made in the opposite direction.
rows.how: Replaced with a stated position and its reasoning on a page of its own: a **parallel, not a branch**, expected to be unrelated and **not yet tested**. **Dismissing a line without looking is exactly as unevidenced as claiming one.**

rows.what: «Nine parishes» on the Archive page
rows.said: «**1,151 registers catalogued across nine parishes**» — the count of books was computed from the data, the count of parishes was typed by hand.
rows.true: There are **fourteen**: Barban, Cerovlje, Gologorica, Gračišće, Ližnjan, Motovun, Pazin, Pićan, Poreč, Svetvinčenat, Umag, Vižinada, Vodnjan and Čepić.
rows.how: Now computed from the same data as the number beside it. **Any figure a page states should be derived, not typed** — a hand-typed number is right on the day it is written and wrong from then on.

rows.what: What the Archive's 1,151 actually counts
rows.said: Nothing false — but the page led with **1,151** and let a reader assume it was a measure of the project's reach. Set beside a sister site's **10,536 records naming 4,779 people**, it invited exactly the wrong comparison.
rows.true: **1,151 counts books, not people.** It is the Pazin inventory of parish registers that exist. This archive has opened a book in **7 of the 14 parishes**, and most of the **997 digitised** volumes have never been looked at. The comparable people-counts are **1,136** on Everyone and **1,508** on The Register.
rows.how: The page now says so in its own words, and says why the sister project's number is larger: it **read a town's death registers act by act** rather than searching an index for one surname. **1,151 is not an achievement. It is the size of the job.**

rows.what: Piero della Francesca in the family tree
rows.said: Nothing on this site — the claim is in **the family's own MyHeritage tree**, which places the painter **Piero della Francesca (1415–1492)** of Sansepolcro in this family, with his father Benedetto and mother Romana di Perino.
rows.true: Piero's father genuinely was a **de' Franceschi** of Sansepolcro, so the surname is real. **The connection to the Carnian and Istrian family is not.** Nothing documents it, and nothing here claims it.
rows.how: Recorded rather than deleted, because the tree is a source this archive reads and it is better to name a doubtful join than to leave it unmentioned. All three are marked so on their own pages. **This is the third famous namesake the project has had to refuse** — after the Venetian printer and the Venetian painter — and the pattern is always the same: a well-known man of the name, and no join but the name.

rows.what: Hedviga Blažević has two birthdays
rows.said: Two pages give her birth as **8 March 1926**. A third page quotes the certified extract of the Senj birth register, attached to her son's 1951 entry, which gives **3 August 1926**.
rows.true: **Both have stood on this site at once and nobody noticed.** Written as numbers they are **8/3/1926** and **3/8/1926** — a day and a month exchanged, almost certainly where a European date met an English-speaking translator. This archive does not know which is right.
rows.how: **Neither has been quietly deleted.** Both now stand, marked as in conflict, and the Senj birth register for 1926 is an errand. The lesson is one this project keeps relearning: **a date that appears twice in an archive should be diffed, not trusted twice.**

rows.what: Anton Rudolf, dead in 1943 and certified in 1950
rows.said: Anton Rudolf Defranceski, born 20 January 1890 at Klenovica house 22, **died in 1943** — recorded here «per the family». The same page also has him **on the Pfullingen list of foreigners in 1947** and **certified by that town's mayor in 1950**.
rows.true: **Those cannot both be about the same living man.** Either the 1943 death is wrong — and it was only ever family testimony, never a register — or the Pfullingen documents are about a different Anton. The archive printed both and did not notice.
rows.how: Surfaced only because the family's oral history of **1948** made the widow's situation matter. Written up on Nineteen forty-eight, and the Crikvenica death register for 1943 is now an errand. **Lore is worth collecting partly because it makes you re-read your own pages.**

rows.what: What the first 403 actually was
rows.said: That FamilySearch's tile server had **blocked** the death-register reading, recorded as `blocked` in the Search Register and written up on Method as a second instance of *when the service says stop, stop*.
rows.true:
**The tile path was wrong.** Tiles live at `…/image.xml`'s sibling `image_files/{level}/{col}_{row}.jpg`, and the reader was asking for `…/{level}/{col}_{row}.jpg` — no `image_files`. Today that same wrong path returns a plain **404**; yesterday the security service answered the unknown path with a **403**. So the reading was stopped by **my own broken URL**, dressed up as somebody else's refusal.

A real block did come later, after several hundred tile requests, on `image.xml` itself — and *that* one is recorded honestly.
rows.how: **Check that the request is well-formed before concluding you have been refused.** A 403 on a path that does not exist is not a verdict on your conduct. The cheap test — does the *correct* URL work? — costs one request and was not run.

rows.what: The FamilySearch paging cap
rows.said: A method note stated the persona endpoint caps out at about **1,100 records**.
rows.true: The real ceiling is about **1,800**. The 1,100 figure came from a run that stopped early and was never retested; the full harvest of 10 September reached 1,800 distinct records before the endpoint began serving page one again.
rows.how: Retested deliberately, at offsets 1,800, 2,600 and 3,600, before publishing a number that the whole of The Register now rests on.

rows.what: Living people
rows.said: The footer of every page read **«Living people are excluded from this build.»**
rows.true: At David's instruction the policy changed: living people the archive knows of are now named, **by name only** — no date of birth, no address, no place of residence, no photograph.
rows.how: The footer was corrected the same day the policy changed, rather than left contradicting the pages above it.

rows.what: A face on the direct line
rows.said: A hand-tinted portrait of a bearded man in a bow tie, published as **Josip Defranceschi, born at Gračišće 22 March 1863** — David's great-grandfather, and the only likeness the direct line had.
rows.true: It is from the **Imotski** branch, and the sitter is a Josip of that family. **No likeness of the Crikvenica Josip is known to this archive.** The companion portrait published as his wife Ana is withdrawn too, because its only identification was that it matched the man beside it.
rows.how: Two branches' photographs sit in one family collection. A card carried the name, this line has a man of that name, and this archive matched the face to the name without asking which Josip — while checking every register plate on the same page against Pazin and Ledenice. **The portrait was never checked against anything.** Identified by David, who holds the originals. The retired 2018 GEDCOM spliced Imotski onto this line as well: the same seam has caught this archive twice.

rows.what: Seventy-eight records moved to the wrong parish
rows.said: That the seventy-eight Vodnjan records were **really Vižinada's**, because resolving them to film 005497893 and asking the catalogue who made that film returned «Rimokatolička crkva. Župa Vižinada».
rows.true: **A reel can carry more than one parish.** That one holds Vižinada's deaths 1754–1831 *and* **Vodnjan's baptisms 1815–1866** (koha:963267). The records are Vodnjan's.
rows.how: The catalogue answers a film-number query with the **first creator on the reel**. The method was sound and the question put to it was wrong. It stood on the site for about an hour, published within twenty minutes of being reached and **without a single image being opened**. What made it look right: the one death on that reel really is Vižinada's — it is in the *Liber Defunctorum of Castellier*, Kaštelir.

rows.what: Forty-four people filed under the wrong town
rows.said: Eight reconstructed Vodnjan households and their children carried **Vižinada** as their parish in the roster, and the households themselves had no place at all.
rows.true: They are Vodnjan. Eight households placed, **forty-four rows moved**, and Vodnjan moved out of *unplaced* into Southern Istria.
rows.how: The correction above was published on the narrative page and **never reached the data**. David asked why the headcount had not moved all day; it had not, because the roster was three commits behind the research and still carried the error the essay had already retracted. Fixed, and the rebuild order is now written into the queue notes.

rows.what: A surname misread
rows.said: «**Alvise Bortolan** q.m Saba», husband of Lucia De Franceschi, in two published entries.
rows.true: «**Alvise Birattan** q.m Saba». The 1825 entry writes it legibly, and the two earlier ones say the same thing once you go back and look.
rows.how: A hard hand read twice from the same wrong first guess. *Bortolan* was this archive's word, not the register's.

rows.what: A marriage dated forty years early
rows.said: Carlo De Franceschi × Maria Michelcich, **1812**.
rows.true: **1 March 1852**, Rovinj, entry 31. The bride was twenty-six, so she cannot have married in 1812.
rows.how: Carried straight from an index whose year field appears to hold the groom's, not the marriage's. It survived because nobody had opened the image — the same failure as the portrait, in a different medium.

rows.what: A broken site pushed live
rows.said: Nothing — the page simply was not there for about six minutes.
rows.true: The build had failed and the commit went out anyway.
rows.how: `npm run build | tail -2` hides the build's exit code behind the pipe's. **This was the second time.** There is now `scripts/publish.sh`, which builds without a pipe, checks that every source page produced an output file, and refuses to commit or push if either fails.

rows.what: An opening said to hold nothing
rows.said: That opening 578 of the Svetvinčenat baptisms holds **no De Franceschi**.
rows.true: It does. The entry was found by resolving the index arks to their images rather than trusting the search result.
rows.how: An absence in an index was read as an absence in the register. The correction was published **underneath the original claim**, which is where it belongs.

rows.what: Two children who are one child
rows.said: Two boys named Piero, baptised nine days apart, counted as two people.
rows.true: One child, entered twice by the priest. The **godparent pair is identical** — Martino Salambat and Andriana Quelis — which is proof, not coincidence.
rows.how: Found by reading the openings rather than the index. The roster had already deduplicated by name and year, so the published count was right for the wrong reason; that too was stated.

rows.what: A petition attributed to the wrong person
rows.said: That the 1942 naturalisation petition filed as «Bruno de Franceschi Or Seedorf» was **Bruno's**.
rows.true: It is **Gerda's** — her declaration, carrying his name in the index because of the marriage.
rows.how: An index heading read as a subject.

rows.what: A column said to be unalignable
rows.said: That the «going to join» entries could not be aligned to the passengers.
rows.true: They align perfectly. **The image holds two ledger pages**, and those particular entries belong to the **Di Bruzzi** family, not to ours.
rows.how: A page boundary mistaken for a data problem.

rows.what: A line described as an open question
rows.said: Vodnjan: «twelve families in 1945 … accounted for by no existing line … the newest open question».
rows.true: **Five documented generations**, two separate lines, and four women of the name married out before the books open.
rows.how: Not wrong when written — overtaken, and left standing for hours after the evidence had changed. The lesson is the same as the roster's: a finding is not published until the data files carry it too.

rows.what: A pedigree spliced at the wrong join
rows.said: The **Imotski** family joined to David's own line, in the 2018 GEDCOM this archive inherited.
rows.true: They are separate. The GEDCOM is retired — 8,286 people against the live tree's 15,643, and David's own verdict: «really old and really wrong».
rows.how: An old export was trusted as a source. It is now used for nothing. Note how often Imotski turns up in this list.

rows.what: A register's own error, kept as it stands
rows.said: «Il Signor Carlo De Franceschi … celibe, **d'anni 40**», 1 March 1852.
rows.true: He was **forty-two**, born 16 October 1809.
rows.how: Not this archive's mistake but the register's, and it is transcribed as written rather than silently improved. Ages in these books are what somebody said in the room — and in this room the man being asked was too ill to stand up.

rows.what: Names that are not this name
rows.said: Nothing — these were caught before publication and are recorded so they are not found again.
rows.true: **Franceschich** of Buzet is a Slavic patronymic, not Franceschi. **Francin** is its own Vodnjan family — although Pietro De Franceschi's first wife was a Francin, so in that parish the two are a household deep in each other. **Pietro Francin q.m Dom.co de Rondel** is not a De Franceschi.
rows.how: Read by eye rather than matched by string. This is the whole argument for reading a register instead of querying one.

rows.what: Bold words breaking onto their own line
rows.said: Nothing wrong in the words — but wherever a paragraph of running prose contained a **bold phrase**, the phrase was thrown onto a line of its own, so the sentence read as three broken fragments.
rows.true: A styling fault, live across the site for an unknown period and on eleven pages that pass marked-up text into a paragraph.
rows.how: `.prose` was declared `display:flex; flex-direction:column`, which turns every inline child — including a `<strong>` — into its own flex item. It is now spacing applied between block children only. Found by looking at a new page rather than by any test. Two stylesheets exist in this repo and only one is loaded; the first fix went into the wrong one.

rows.what: Counting records by place, with a parameter that does not count
rows.said: Per-place record counts for this surname across sixty Istrian and Kvarner towns, and a research queue carrying «Vižinada — 53 records, unread», «Draguč — 25», «Dubrovnik — 38».
rows.true: **The place parameter on this search endpoint does not filter.** Ten values were tested, including «Zzzznowhere» and «Atlantis», and every one returned the same total: **3,652**. Vižinada and Draguč return identical result sets. Dubrovnik returns the unfiltered list. The queued «Vižinada 53» records are on the **Vodnjan** film and have already been read.
rows.how: The parameter is a relevance boost dressed as a filter — no error, no warning, just the whole set back in a different order. The sweep survives because its method independently checked each record's own place text before counting it; the **queue did not**, and carried three phantom tasks for days. The reliable route is to resolve records to their film and read the catalogue's item list — remembering that a film can carry more than one parish.

rows.what: «Never once as the officiant»
rows.said: That Don Stefano De Franceschi appears in the Vodnjan marriage register **nineteen times as a witness and never once as the officiant** — a point this archive made repeatedly, because it fixed his standing under the parroco Giovanni Tromba.
rows.true: On **26 January 1833** he married a couple himself: «**D.n Stefano De Franceschi, De Parochi lic., li congiunse e benedisse nella Chiesa Parrocchiale**».
rows.how: True of every entry from 1819 to the end of 1832, and stated as though it were true of the whole book — while sixty openings of that book were still unread. **A claim about a register nobody has finished reading is a claim about the part you have read.** What survives is the better point: he acts «De Parochi lic.», by the parish priest's licence, exactly as at the baptism of 1816. Seventeen years apart, the same three words.

rows.what: Reading a formula as a personal arrangement
rows.said: That «**De Parochi lic.**» — by the parish priest's licence — was the particular standing Don Stefano De Franceschi held at Vodnjan, and that the register used «the same three words about him» seventeen years apart, at a baptism in 1816 and at an altar in 1833.
rows.true: It is the register's **standard formula for any priest deputising for the parroco**. The very next entry, 13 February 1833, uses it of **Don Pietro Bradamante**.
rows.how: Published the day before, on a run of entries that happened to feature one man. Two consecutive days of the same book undid it. The underlying fact is unchanged — Don Stefano was never the parson of Vodnjan — but the phrase was doing work it does not do.

rows.what: Publishing this archive's own method back to it as a discovery
rows.said: That forty-five per cent of the indexed records carry no town, that the film number in each record is the way to a parish, and — presented as the day's lesson — that a reel can carry more than one parish, so the film is «a fast first pass and not an answer».
rows.true:
**All three were already on this site.** The parish-map section of the same page says the index «usually gives no parish… every persona carries the ark of the image it was read from, the service turns that ark into a DGS film number, and the catalogue names the film's parish». And the correction entry above it, from 9 September, already ends: «The reliable route is to resolve records to their film and read the catalogue's item list — *remembering that a film can carry more than one parish*.»

The 45% is a measurement of something this archive had already stated qualitatively. It was written up as though nobody here had noticed.
rows.how:
By not reading the page being added to. Four sections were appended to /istria-sweep/ in one afternoon without the existing parish-map section being read first — the same page, eighty lines further down.

**What is actually new, and it is narrower:** `q.fatherSurname` and `q.motherSurname` are honoured when either is the sole name term, which the reference note said was impossible and which took the pool from 954 records to 1,619; and resolving a record through its **image ark to the book waypoint** is finer than film-to-catalogue — it settles a two-parish reel *automatically* instead of requiring somebody to remember to check. The measurement that 110 of 112 records on film 005497893 are the second parish's is new. The idea is not.

rows.what: «The earliest the surname is indexed anywhere in Istria: Labin, 1615»
rows.said: That an **Aloÿsius Defranceschi** appears at Albona in **1615** — «sixty-four years before the Mione headmen's list, and eighty-five before the date Carlo gives for his family's arrival». Carried as one of three key findings of the September sweep, pinned on the atlas, and used as the outer bound of the family's presence in Istria.
rows.true:
**Three later measurements cannot find it.** The **rebuilt sweep** on the same page — written precisely because the first method matched a truncated field and stopped early — gives Labin **1789–1892**. The **by-image test** of 13 September gives **1826–1866**, and six of Labin's fourteen indexed hits are *Franceschich*, *Francescich*, *Francocich*, which are not this family. And this archive's own **register**, 1,508 rows each carrying the id the service returned for it, **holds no 1615 Labin row**; its only 1615 row is an *Andriana Franchini*.

So the 1615 exists in one place only: the table built by the method this page has already declared broken. **And the source of the number has since been found.** The only *Aloÿsius Defranceschi* in any harvest on disk is born **1790**, son of *Mathæus Defranceschi and Osvalda Labinaz or Dominj* — a **Vižinada** household. The *Gasparo De Franceschi* named beside him is in none of the data. And Labin's filmed volume list contains a book called «**Deaths (Umrli) 1615, 1585-1649**».

So the entry was a man from the wrong parish dated two centuries early, a man who does not exist, and **a date taken from a shelf-list instead of a record**. It is withdrawn, not merely disputed.

**What stands instead: Rovinj 1619, then Svetvinčenat 1628.** Both are in the register, both have an image behind them, and the second was read off the page the same morning.
rows.how:
By checking a load-bearing number against the archive's own data instead of against the page that first published it. The check cost one grep. It was prompted by writing a new place page for Labin and finding nothing in the register to put on it.

**Withdrawn the same day** after searching every harvest file for the name rather than only the published tables. That search cost one grep too, and should have been the first thing done rather than the second.

rows.what: Ten women shown as born in the year their own children were being baptised
rows.said: A birth year for each of ten married-in women — «b. 1822» for Lucia Bonassin, «b. 1816» for Maria Malusá, «b. 1841» for Maria Dorliguzzo, and seven more.
rows.true:
**None of those is a birth year.** Each woman is the *mother* of a household whose first child is baptised in that very year, or in one of the years she was already bearing children. Lucia Bonassin «b. 1822» is the mother in «Gio Maria De Franceschi × Lucia Bonassin, **1822**–1831». Maria Malusá «b. 1816» is the mother in «Pietro De Franceschi × Maria Malusá, **1816**–1824». Anna Defranceschi (Voran) «b. 1865» is the mother in a household running **1857–1865**.

The year is the first time she appears in the record — the baptism of her eldest known child. It was carried into the roster as a birth. **Nobody is born in the year their own child is born.**

All ten now show the year as a first appearance, with the birth recorded as unknown.
rows.how:
Found by asking why the pedigree gate was suppressing fifty-five charts. The gate was doing its job: it refuses a parent who would be under twelve at the first birth, and these women were failing that test **because their data said they were nought.** The charts were the symptom; the birth years were the fault.

**And one rule was tried and withdrawn inside the same hour.** Generalising it — *any* person whose recorded birth is less than twelve years before a household they parent — «corrected» **113 rows**, including an Antonio Defranceschi born 1897 attached to an 1825 household and a Josip Defranceski born 1947 attached to one from 1890. Those are not bad birth years; they are **name collisions**, which this archive proved the same morning when «Maria Defranceschi» turned out to be thirteen women in thirteen parishes. The rule assumed the match was right and the year wrong; in 103 of 113 cases it was the other way round. Reverted, and narrowed to the one case where the name form itself identifies a wife — «Maiden (Married)» — which no father and son can share.

rows.what: «Gio Batta De Franceschi and Zanetta Gravisi, parents of the groom»
rows.said: That the Šterna household ran **Gio Batta De Franceschi × Zanetta Gravisi**, and that their son Bortolo's marriage stood behind two entries in the book of 1723–1820. Published on the morning of 13 September, on the strength of the index's four names.
rows.true:
**Zanetta Gravisi is Bortolo's wife, not his mother.** The index lists groom, groom's father, bride and bride's father; this archive read four names as two couples.

The page reads: «Bortolo figlio del q. Gio: Batta de Franceschi **dalla Cargna**… ha contratto legitimo Matrimonio coll'Ill.ma Sig.a **Zanetta Gravisi** figlia dell'Ill.mo Sig.r **Marchese Nazario** della Villa di Cepich di questa Pieve», 12 November 1777.

And there was never a second marriage. The other «record» is a modern **archivist's pencil finding-aid slip** filmed with the book, which the index counted as a separate entry — and which independently confirms every word of the reading.
rows.how:
By opening the two images instead of reasoning about the index rows, which is what the same page had already said was the only reliable move. The correction was published the same day as the claim.

It is also the most valuable correction this archive has made, because going to the page produced the sentence the whole project has been missing: **an Istrian De Franceschi whose origin is written down**.

rows.what: Ten more birth years that are first-appearance dates
rows.said: Birth years for ten people who are parents in a Vodnjan household — «b. 1817» and «b. 1819» for a Pietro De Franceschi whose household runs 1816–1824, «b. 1822» and «b. 1830» for a Domenica whose household runs 1817–1832, and so on.
rows.true: Each year falls **inside the span during which that household was baptising children**, and each person is a parent in it. They are first-appearance dates. Twenty such years have now been corrected across the site.
rows.how:
The earlier pass used only the name form «Maiden (Married)», which is safe but narrow. This one adds two tests that let the rule reach further without repeating the morning's mistake of blanking 113 good years:

**The places must agree.** A row at Draguč matched to a household at Rijeka is a name collision, not a bad year — 59 of 121 candidates failed this and were left alone.

**The year must fall inside the childbearing span.** Place agreement is not enough on its own, because Vodnjan recycles the same six Christian names across generations: a *Pietro De Franceschi b. 1858* sits at the same place as a Pietro whose household ran 1816–1824, and he is a grandson, not a bad date. **Eighteen were skipped on this test**, all but three of them at Vodnjan.

Ten survived both. The rule is now narrow enough to state: a person who is a parent in a household, at the same place, whose recorded birth falls within the years that household was bearing children, has a first appearance recorded as a birth.

rows.what: «Francisca Defranceschi × Antonius Cerneca, nine children 1831–1846»
rows.said: That the largest of the married-out daughters had nine children by an Antonius Cerneca between 1831 and 1846. Published this morning as the head of the lost-daughters queue.
rows.true:
**Her husband is Joannes Bergamo, and they are not children.** The Svetvinčenat marriage book after 1815 is a ruled table with four printed column headings — SPONSI, SPONSAE, **GENITORES SPONSI**, **GENITORES SPONSAE** — and the index flattens all four parents into one list. *«Vincentius Bergamo, son of Joannes Bergamo and Francisca Defranceschi, marries Euphemia Cerneca, daughter of Antonius Cerneca and Joanna Ferrara»* arrives as one row of five names, and this archive read names three and four as the husband.

The five rows are the **weddings of four sons** — Joannes 1831, Dominicus 1836, Vincentius 1840, Antonius 1846 — not nine baptisms.

She remains a married-out daughter; that part of the queue's logic is unaffected. **Every husband in this archive inferred from an `o` list on a post-1815 marriage register is now suspect.**
rows.how:
By opening the page. The column headings are printed in capitals across the top of every opening and settle it in one look. The same morning's own text had already said that the reliable move is to read the register rather than the index; it took until the afternoon to apply that to a row this archive had itself put at the top of a queue.

**Bergamo is also the point.** Kandler lists the Carnian families at Sanvincenti as Defranceschi, Lupieri, Fiorencis, Fabris, Crosilla and Bergamo — so this is two Carnian houses intermarrying, which the wrong husband had hidden.

rows.what: «A Bartolo buried in July 1819, which is Bortolo himself at the end of it»
rows.said: That the Šterna burial of July 1819 closed the life of Bortolo de Franceschi, the man who came from Carnia and married Zanetta Gravisi in 1777.
rows.true: The entry **names parents** — «Bartolo De Franceschi, of Gio: Batta De Franceschi and Maria». A burial that names a father and mother is a child's. This is a **grandson** carrying the grandfather's name, in the second Gio: Batta's household. **Bortolo's own death has not been found.**
rows.how: By reading what the index row actually said rather than what the page's narrative wanted. The same hour's work also found that Šterna's registers **begin in 1667, not 1723** — a composite first volume of 207 images — and that **it holds no De Franceschi at all**, which is the negative result the Carnia entry predicts.

rows.what: Every mother one generation too deep on the ancestor chart
rows.said: An ancestor chart published a few hours earlier, in which **Hedviga Blažević was drawn as Ivan Defranceski's mother**, Uršula Kovačina as Anton Rudolf's mother, Anna Kalanj as Josip's mother, Maria Fernasar as Antonio's, and Francisca Salomon as Giovanni Battista's.
rows.true:
**Each of those women is the wife of the man she was drawn under, not his mother.** The whole maternal side of the chart was shifted by one generation. A wife belongs above her *children*, not above her husband — Anna Kalanj is Anton Rudolf's mother, not Josip's; Hedviga Blažević is the mother of the living generation, not of the man she married.

Rebuilt so that each couple's children sit below them: **I. Defranceski ← Ivan (1925–1995) and Hedviga Blažević**; **Ivan ← Anton Rudolf and Uršula Kovačina**; **Anton Rudolf ← Josip and Anna Kalanj**; **Josip ← Antonio and Maria Fernasar**; **Antonio ← Giovanni Battista and Francisca Salomon**. Giovanni Battista's own mother is now a wall, because she is genuinely not named anywhere.
rows.how:
By printing the tree as a list of [role] pairs instead of looking at the rendered chart. On the screen the error is nearly invisible — every box is in a plausible place and every name is right. On one line of text per person, with «father» or «mother» against each, it is obvious in a second.

The lesson is the same one this archive keeps relearning in a different costume: **a shape that looks right is not a check.** The descent view built from the same data was correct throughout, which is why the error survived — the two views disagreed and nobody had asked them to agree.

rows.what: The Atlas was drawing a fifth of what the archive knows, and this site holds two different Gračišćes
rows.said: The Atlas carried **52 hand-written pins** and had done since it was built. The dek said «every place this archive can put a document in», which was not true: the roster names **266 place strings** attaching **1,440 people** to the ground.
rows.true:
Rebuilt from the roster, the map holds **154 places and 955 people**. Three things were wrong rather than merely missing.

· **One town was being drawn several times under different names.** Almissa and Omiš are the same place; so are Fiume, Vitipolis and Tarsatica, which is why the first rebuild put **Rijeka on the map three times**. Historic and Italian forms are now folded onto the town they name.

· **This archive holds two different coordinates for Gračišće**, seven kilometres apart — one in *places.json*, one in *atlas.json*. Neither was flagged because nothing had ever compared them. The heavier pin keeps the ground and the builder now refuses to draw one name twice.

· **Seventy-three entries name something that is not a town.** Thirteen say «Österreich», five «Austria», four «Italy»; and four each say **«Santa Maria Assunta», «Immacolata Concezione» and «Assunzione di Maria Santissima»** — church dedications written into a place field. Those are left off the map and are a data error to be cleaned, not a place to be pinned.
rows.how: Found by building the thing properly rather than by checking it. Nothing compares a gazetteer against itself until something has to draw both.

rows.what: «642 volumes open at page one» — the Carnian ones do not open at all
rows.said: Published this morning: «985 more volumes now open at page one», counting **343 Dalmatian and 642 Carnian**. The Carnian half was described exactly like the Croatian half.
rows.true:
**The images of the entire Udine collection are restricted.** The viewer answers *«Image Restricted — access is typically determined by local laws or the custodian»*. Tested at **Colza, Comeglians and Paluzza**; all three are shut. The Croatian volumes — Istria, the Kvarner and Dalmatia — open normally, which is how the mistake survived a spot-check: the one volume tested end to end that morning was **Tinjan**, and Tinjan is Croatian.

So the honest count is **652 volumes that open** and **642 that are addressable but gated**. The link is still worth having — it names the exact volume and its register number, which is what a reading-room request needs — but it is a catalogue entry, not a document.
rows.how: Found within hours, by going to do the thing the page promised: reading Colza to settle whether Ovaro's registers are filed under it. **The page said the volume was open; the volume was shut.** A link was tested for the wrong country and the claim was written for both.

rows.what: «Settling Ovaro means a reading room» — it means a browser, and always did
rows.said: Published hours earlier, on finding FamilySearch's Udine images restricted: *«Settling Ovaro now means a Family History Center, an affiliate library, or the Archivio di Stato di Udine itself — not an afternoon at a screen.»*
rows.true:
**The Archivio di Stato di Udine has published them itself, on Antenati, free and open.** Ovaro has **271 registers** there and **fifty-nine of them are Mione's**, catalogued under its own name.

The first correction was right about FamilySearch and wrong about the world. **One vendor's gate was mistaken for the state of the record.**

The reason it was missed is worth keeping: Antenati was searched **by name**, which returns nothing for Tolmezzo, because only part of the holding is name-indexed. The portal says so on the results page. **The registers were one form away the whole time.**
rows.how: Found by retrying a source this archive had twice written off — once as «403s both browsers», once as «needs a reading room» — and by reading the failure message instead of accepting it.

rows.what: «Antenati has the Mione registers all along» — this archive already knew, on its own Carnia page
rows.said: Published this afternoon: that Mione's fifty-nine registers are open on Antenati and that «this archive has been saying for months that they were not online».
rows.true:
**The Carnia page already said it**, in as many words: *«The Archivio di Stato di Udine has digitised the Napoleonic civil registers of the Comune di Mione — fifty-nine volumes… and publishes them openly on the Antenati portal.»* It had already read the 1809 and 1810 birth books and published four households out of them.

What was actually new this afternoon was narrower and should have been stated as such: **the 1806 volume had not been read**, and it holds a fifth household and a generation above it.

The error was mine and it was the ordinary one — **I searched the web before I searched the archive.** A site of twelve hundred pages will tell you what it already knows if you ask it first.
rows.how: Caught within the hour, by grepping this archive's own data before writing up the register act.

rows.what: «Mione and Muina are both done, and both are closed» — Mione has twelve allegati, not two
rows.said: Published this evening, as the closing note on the Ovaro marriage allegati: *«Mione and Muina are both done, and both are closed.»*
rows.true:
**Mione is not closed.** The Antenati register browser returns its results ten to a page, and I read page one. Page one carries two Mione files. **Pages two and three carry ten more** — 1808, 1809 (two files), 1810 (two), 1811 (two), 1812, 1813, 1814 and 1815. Only the 1806 file had been read.

Ovaro itself has eight further allegati on those same pages, and none of them had been counted either.

The error was the shape of the tool, not the archive: **a paginated result set answered as though it were the whole set.** The fix is the obvious one — page to the end before saying «all».
rows.how: Caught the same evening, going back for the remaining village files and finding the count did not match.

rows.what: «Both alive in 1808» — Antonio de Franceschi of Muina was dead before his son's wedding
rows.said: The Muina chain said of Antonio de Franceschi and Maria née Corva: *«Farmers of Muina. **Both alive in 1808**: Antonio gave his written consent to his son's marriage on 25 October 1807, three months before the wedding.»*
rows.true:
**Antonio was dead by the wedding day.** The marriage allegati of Mione 1808 — the loose documents the couple actually produced — style the groom *«Osvaldo del fu Antonio de Franceschi»* and take a separate consent from *«Donna Maria nata Corva, **vedova** del fu Antonio de Franceschi»*. Under the Napoleonic Code a mother's consent was required only where the father had died, so the existence of that second act is itself the proof.

The error came from the marriage act's phrase *«figlio di Antonio de Franceschi, e di Maria nata Corva, **pure agricoltori**»* — «also farmers». That names a trade, not a living man, and it was read as though the present tense covered both parents.

**The correction yields a fact the archive did not have.** Antonio's written consent is dated 25 October 1807 and his widow's consent 28 January 1808: **he died inside those fourteen weeks**, bracketed by two documents, neither of which is a death record.
rows.how: Caught by reading the allegati themselves instead of the register's summary of them — and only because the file had been wrongly counted as read.

rows.what: «Nave, a hamlet of Mione» — the clerks attach it to Luincis too
rows.said: Published this evening: that **Nave** is *«a hamlet, not of Mione at large»*, on the strength of «De Franceschi de Nave Mionensis», «Giorgi de Nave Mionensis» and «Micoli-Toscano de Nave Mionensis».
rows.true:
Three hours later the **Lenzone** file produced **«Fiorenzi de Nave Luincis»** — the same locality given with a *different* village. Nave is therefore **not a sub-division of Mione**; it is a small place in the Ovaro cluster that the clerks attached to Mione and to Luincis alike.

The substance is unaffected: a De Franceschi household and the Micoli Toscano are recorded in the same small place. Only the administrative description was wrong, and it was wrong because it was written from three documents that all happened to say «Mionensis».
rows.how: Caught the same evening by reading a neighbouring village's file — which is the whole argument for reading all of them.

rows.what: «Giovanni Pietro Antonio Cramaro, born 1758» — he was an ERMAN, born 1752, and «cramaro» was his father's trade
rows.said: Published this afternoon, from the 1809 marriage allegati: that Orsola de Franceschi was bundled with the baptismal extract of **«Giovanni Pietro Antonio Cramaro», born 28 April 1758**, «almost certainly the groom», and that **«the name Cramaro is worth a second look»** because the *cramars* were the Carnian pedlars and «a De Franceschi daughter marries a man whose family name **is** that road».
rows.true:
**The pairing was right. The name was not, and neither was the year.**

The marriage act itself — Mione, Matrimoni 1809, act N. 1, read this evening — gives the groom as **«Erman de Franceschi Gio: Pietro»**, aged fifty-six, son of the late **Pietro Erman** and **Maddalena née de Franceschi**, and reads his birth act as **28 April 1752**. He signs himself **«Gio: Pietro Erman de Franceschi»**.

The priest's extract had said *«figlio di Pietro **cramaro** del villaggio di Mione»* — **Pietro the cramar**, the trade, lower-case, standing where a byname goes in these registers. This archive read a trade as a surname and then built a paragraph on it.

The birth year was a second, smaller error of the same kind: **the last digit had been cropped out of the magnified image and was guessed at from context.**

**The truth is better than the mistake.** The family Orsola married into is **Erman** — and «Zuane d'Erman» is one of the three men in the 1679 list who went from Mione to Istria with Zuane De Franceschi. The two families were still marrying each other a hundred and thirty years later, and the groom's own mother was a de Franceschi already.
rows.how: Caught by going to the marriage register instead of stopping at the allegati — which is the rule this archive should have been following: read the loose papers to find the marriage, read the register to believe it.

rows.what: «Two instruments, two companies, one century» — the DNA convergence this archive published tonight does not exist
rows.said: Published this evening, as the headline of the 23andMe section: that David's **0.2% Southern Indian & Sri Lankan** is *«1/512 — nine generations, about 1750–1780»*, that this is *«the window this page reasoned to from the Y chromosome alone, before the trace was known»*, and that **«two instruments, two companies, one century… is a convergence, and it is the strongest thing on this page.»**
rows.true:
**There is no convergence. The trace is maternal.**

Both of David's parents share their 23andMe results with him, and the comparison panels say it plainly: **Ivan 0.0% Central & South Asian. Cheryl 0.5%. David 0.2%** — half his mother's, as inheritance requires. The **Sub-Saharan African** behaves the same way: Cheryl 0.8%, Ivan 0.0%, David 0.3%.

The trace comes down the **mother's** line. **L-M27 comes down the father's.** They have nothing to do with one another, and the arithmetic that joined them joined two unrelated numbers.

**The consequence is not neutral — it makes the Y finding starker.** Ivan is **99.9% European** with no non-European trace at all, and he carries L-M27 on two companies' chips. The haplogroup now has **no autosomal corroboration whatever**.
rows.how: Caught the same evening, by reading the parents' kits. **The failure was not the reading — it was the publishing.** The same article said, three paragraphs below the claim, *«Which parent the trace came from is not yet known… Ivan's own 23andMe kit will answer it free»* — and then ran the convergence as the headline anyway. **A stated caveat is not permission to lean on the conclusion.** The check took two clicks inside an account this archive was already signed into.

rows.what: «Salante» — the bride of 1808 was a GALANTE, and the marriage register says so twice
rows.said: This archive has carried **Appolonia Salante**, daughter of **Antonio Salante** and Speranza née Micoli, for months — in the Muina chain, the 1806 households table, the plate caption for the marriage act, the dossiers and the open questions. And this morning, faced with the notary writing **Galante** twice, it doubled down: *«This archive keeps Salante, because that is what the parish book and the register say, and the register is what the family was entered under.»*
rows.true:
**The register does not say Salante. It says Galante, twice.**

Mione, Matrimoni 1808, act N. 1, read this evening: *«…ed **Appolonia Galante** villica di professione, dell'età d'anni venticinque e mezzo, figlia di **Antonio Galante** e di Speranza nata Micoli»* — in the same clear looped G the notary used.

**The count is now four hands to two.** For **Galante**: the notary Giacomo Micoli in both of his consent acts of 1808, the marriage register in both of its mentions, and **Pietro Galante signing his own name** at Mione in 1813 in a plain lower-case g. For **Salante**: the parish priest's baptismal extract, and the clerk who docketed the allegati file.

The name has been changed to **Galante** throughout — the Muina chain, the households table, the plate caption, the dossiers and the questions. The priest's *Salante* is kept on the record as what he wrote, because he was copying from the baptismal book and that is where the variant lives.
rows.how: Caught by reading the 1808 marriage register instead of quoting it from memory. **The claim that «the register says Salante» was never checked against the register** — it was inherited from an earlier transcription of the same act and then asserted as evidence against fresh, better readings.

rows.what: Where Osvaldo the elder's death is not: the Mione civil death register does not begin early enough
rows.said: Nothing wrong was published. This is recorded so the search is not repeated.
rows.true:
The 1806 death register for the Comune di Mione holds **one act**: a Brenci child of three years and nine months, died 18 November, registered 20 November 1806 by **Giovanni Micoli-Toscano**.

**That is the whole volume.** Civil death registration at Mione effectively begins in **November 1806**.

Osvaldo the elder consented in writing to his daughter's marriage on **7 September 1805** and was *«il fu Osvaldo»* by **August 1806**. **His death therefore falls before the civil series starts**, and no amount of reading Antenati will produce it.

**It can only be in the parish register of the Pieve di Gorto** — the same book every baptismal extract in these files was copied out of. That moves the Pieve books from «worth having» to «the only route».
rows.how: Established by reading the volume rather than assuming the series was continuous from 1806.

rows.what: Anna, wife of Paolo de Franceschi, was not born to the surname
rows.said: Published 14 September 2026: that the 1815 death act's **«Anna de Franceschi … maritata col suddetto Paolo de Franceschi»** admits two readings — that she was born a de Franceschi, as the 1808 act's *«Giovanna pure de Franceschi»* shows is possible at Mione, or that the clerk entered a married woman under her husband's surname — and that this archive would not choose between them without a second document.
rows.true:
