**The second document turned up the next day, and it chooses.** The Mione banns of **4 June 1815** — five months before she died — publish the marriage of her son and name her **«Anna nata Brunis»**.

She **married into** the surname. The endogamy reading is wrong for this couple.

What survives: the 1808 act still says *«pure de Franceschi»* in as many words, so **one** De Franceschi–De Franceschi marriage at Mione stands. Not two.

*The maiden surname is read as **Brunis**; **Brencis**, already documented in this village, cannot be excluded at this resolution.*

rows.what: Which Osvaldo de Franceschi witnessed the two Muina deaths of 1814
rows.said: Published 14 September 2026: that the *«Osvaldo de Franceschi d'anni ventisette, Servitore»* who identified two bodies at Muina in September and November 1814 could be either **the carpenter of Mione** or **a second Osvaldo at Muina**, that the question was unresolved, and — as a stated opinion, not a finding — that his **signature** looked to me like the same hand as the Mione carpenter's of 1809.
rows.true:
**The 1808 banns, read the next day, shift it decisively to the Muina man — and the signature remark should be withdrawn.**

The second Osvaldo is **Osvaldo de Franceschi of Muina, born 14 March 1788**, son of Antonio q.m Leonardo and Maria née Corva — a man this archive already held, and whom I failed to put in the frame.

**The village fits** (the 1814 witnesses are *neighbours at Muina*; the carpenter is *«di Mione»*). **The trade fits better** (*agricoltore* → *servitore*, against *falegname* → *servitore*). **And the age fits exactly**: born 14 March 1788, he is nineteen years ten months on 17 January 1808 and the banns say **twenty**; twenty-six and a half in September 1814 and twenty-six and eight months in November, and both acts say **twenty-seven**. The same rounding, six years apart.

**The handwriting observation is retired rather than defended.** Two men who learned to write in the same valley write alike; that is what I was looking at. The hedge was correct and the lean was not.

*Still short of proof — this is an inference, and it is graded as one.*

rows.what: Thirty-four Kvarner parishes reported as never walked, when they had been
rows.said: Published on the Research Map's first build: that **thirty-four of the forty Kvarner parishes carry only a browse link and no volume list at all**, that the rebuild was what made this visible, and that those thirty-four were first in the queue for enumeration. The page's coverage figure was given as **111 of 1,196 places and 590 volumes**.
rows.true:
**They had all been walked, and the fault was in my own builder.**

Kvarner keeps its volume lists under a field called **`films`** — the same as Dalmatia — and carries a stale `books` title-list on **six** of its forty parishes. The build script read `books` for Kvarner and `films` for Dalmatia, so thirty-four parishes with full inventories came through as empty.

**Corrected figures: 140 of 1,196 places walked, and 777 volumes inventoried** — not 111 and 590. Kvarner's 255 volumes are on the map, with links that open each book at its first image.

This was caught within the hour, and only because David asked me to start work on the thirty-four. *The instruction was sound; the premise I had given him was not.*

rows.what: Two links on the Research Map printed as literal square brackets
rows.said: The page's main paragraph carried two internal links written in markdown — **[Logged as a correction](/corrections/)** among them. Both rendered on the live site exactly as typed, brackets, parentheses and all.
rows.true:
**The archive's markup renderer has no link syntax and never had one.** `md.js` handles bold, italic and «quotes», deliberately, so that data files stay plain. Writing a markdown link into one of those strings does not fail loudly — it just prints.

Fixed on the page rather than in the shared renderer: the two links are resolved locally and put through the same base-path helper as every other internal link, so no other page inherits a syntax it was not written for. **The correction that this page pointed at was unreachable for as long as the link was broken**, which is the part that actually mattered.

rows.what: Matricula Online listed in the plan as a source for Senj and Karlobag
rows.said: The research map's plan named **Matricula Online** as a fifth provider to be built in, *«(Senj, Karlobag)»*.
rows.true:
**Matricula holds no Croatian parish at all.** Its fonds index lists Germany, Austria, Poland, Serbia, Luxembourg, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Italy and Switzerland, and its place search returns nothing for Senj, Karlobag, Rijeka or Fiume.

That line was written from memory and never checked before it went into the plan. **The map has four providers, not five**, and the item is struck rather than left to look like outstanding work.

rows.what: Antenati's ark numbering assumed to run one comune per block
rows.said: The first build of the Antenati catalogue named **fifty-nine volumes for Mione and Ovaro** from contiguous ark ranges, on the assumption that the portal numbers its registers a comune at a time. Series spans were written from that assumption, and one range — an_ua679984 to 679991 — was given to Ovaro's marriages outright.
rows.true:
**It does not number that way.** Walking each ark's own catalogue page showed that **an_ua667510 to 667513 are Mieli, a different comune** — Morti 1807, Nati 1806, Nati 1807 — sitting immediately before Mione's marriages in the numbering.

The catalogue is rebuilt from **forty-six arks actually fetched and read**, plus the eleven this archive has opened act by act. Every volume now carries **how its identity is known** — walked, read, or unconfirmed — and five arks inside Mione's range are listed as unconfirmed rather than given a year they might not have.

**The Mione inference survived the check.** Matrimoni, allegati, indici and pubblicazioni came back exactly as predicted, 1807 missing from each. The Ovaro range did not survive and is withdrawn: only the two Ovaro volumes this archive has actually read are claimed.

*The page stood for under two hours.* It was checked because a single probe — the very first ark fetched — came back Mieli.

rows.what: «1807 is absent from every series in both comuni» — Ovaro has it
rows.said: Published on the Carnia page and written into the Pieve di Gorto errand: that **1807 is missing from every series at Mione and at Ovaro**, and that there is *«no 1807 marriage volume, at Mione or at Ovaro»*.
rows.true:
**Ovaro's 1807 marriage register is on Antenati** — ark an_ua679983 — and Ovaro's marriages run **1806 to 1815 with no gap at all**. Its 1807 allegati survive too (an_ua679993).

The claim was written from the Mione inventory and extended to Ovaro **before Ovaro had been walked**. Walking it took twenty-five fetches and contradicted the sentence.

**The correction makes the finding stronger, not weaker.** A year missing from one comune while the next comune up the valley kept it is not a failure of the system in 1807 — it is **one lost volume**, and that is a thing an archivist can be asked about.

rows.what: Anna Cecilia de Franceschi's death given as 28 January 1810, and her age as a month
rows.said: Published twice. First from the death act alone: *«Morti 1810, act N. 1 — **28 January 1810**, eight in the evening»*, and — reading the registrar's *«un mese circa»* as a fact — **«born about December 1809»**. Then again after the birth act was found, as **«dead at one month on 28 January»**.
rows.true:
**She died on 25 January 1810, eleven days old.**

The act opens *«Comune di Mione **li 25 Venticinque Gennajo** mille ottocento dieci»* — the number in figures and spelled out, agreeing. And the birth act of the same register series has her **born Sunday 14 January 1810 at three in the morning**.

**The «un mese circa» is the registrar's own error**, not evidence. Giacomo Micoli wrote both acts eleven days apart and guessed the age of a child whose birth he had himself recorded. This archive then built a December 1809 birth on that guess, and kept the wrong death date even after finding the real birth.

*The lesson is the one this page keeps relearning: **an age in these acts is a guess and a date is a record**, and where they disagree the date wins.*

rows.what: The research map's «Nothing filmed here» filter could never show anything
rows.said: The map offered five colours, one of them grey for **«Nothing filmed here»**. Clicking it showed **0 of 1,187 places**, every time. The legend said the state existed and the map said it did not.
rows.true:
**Two faults, and the second matters more than the first.**

The builder dropped any place with no provider block before it reached the map — which is precisely the set the grey colour was meant to show. **Three places were being silently discarded**; they are now on the all-providers view.

**And the label was a lie.** Two of the three are **Evangelical**, and they are not unfilmed — **this archive never found the Evangelical root in FamilySearch's waypoint tree**, so that shelf was never walked. The colour is now «in no catalogue at all», the panel on those two markers says the fault is ours, and [finding the Evangelical root](/worklist/) is on the work list.

rows.what: The research map coloured its markers by how many volumes a parish holds
rows.said: Published this morning, and defended in prose: that shading by **depth** — one or two volumes, three to nine, ten or more — was the fix for a colour scale that had saturated. The legend read *«One or two volumes»*, *«Three to nine»*, *«Ten or more»*.
rows.true:
**It answered a question nobody was asking.** A parish with forty volumes nobody has opened and a parish with two nobody has opened are in **exactly the same state**, and the map was spending its only visual channel on the difference between them.

The colour now says **how far this archive has got**: catalogued and never opened, started, read right through. Depth has not been lost — it is in the panel, in words, where *«114 volumes catalogued»* can sit beside *«nobody has opened any of it»* without either pretending to be the other.

**The honest picture is worse than the one it replaced**: 1,219 places catalogued and untouched, 20 started, **none finished**, and 16 volumes of 7,159 read one at a time. That is the number the map exists to show.

*Third scale in two days.* The first saturated, the second was pretty and wrong, and this one was David's correction, not mine.

rows.what: A family archive that did not name the compiler's own brother-in-law, cousins, wife or children
rows.said: The archive's rule has been published since 10 September: *«living relatives are listed by name only — no date of birth, no address, no place of residence, no photograph»*. It read as a policy being applied. **It was naming exactly two living people**: David and his mother.
rows.true:
**Every import this archive has ever run was built to find the dead.** Parish registers, headstones, a reconstructed census, a surname harvest of a family tree filtered to people with death dates. Nothing in that machinery would ever have returned a living cousin, and nobody noticed, because the rule about living people looked like the reason they were absent when in fact they had never been looked for.

**Ten people added**, name only: David's father's sister and brother, his uncle and aunt by marriage, three first cousins, his wife, and his two sons — who are **generation 9 of the direct line** and were not on a site about their own family.

*Found because David looked at his own tree beside this site and asked where everybody was.* The dead had four hundred years of coverage and the living had two names.

rows.what: «Erman is a by-name on a De Franceschi house» — published as a discovery the archive had already made better
rows.said: Written up on reading Mione's Morti for 1810: that the man who signs **«Erman De Franceschi Gio: Pietro»** undoes a distinction this archive had been making, that *«the register does not keep the two names apart, and neither does he»*, and that **the plainest reading is a by-name on a De Franceschi house** — with a note that every page treating Erman and De Franceschi as separate families needed correcting.
rows.true:
**The archive had the answer already, on the same page, from a better document.**

His **marriage act of 1809** — read and published here days earlier — gives him as *«son of the late **Pietro Erman** and **Maddalena née de Franceschi**»*. **The compound surname is simply his two parents**, an Erman father and a De Franceschi mother carried together. That is ordinary Carnian practice and it needs no by-name, no re-reading of the 1679 list, and no correction of any other page.

The 1810 signatures are still worth having — they are the fourth and fifth time he writes his own name — but they confirm rather than reveal.

*The failure was not in the reading.* It was in treating a volume read end to end as if it arrived in an empty archive. **Reading carefully is no protection against forgetting what is already held.**

rows.what: «154 volumes that exist on a shelf in Istria and cannot be read from anywhere else»
rows.said: A page built this afternoon around Pazin's «not digitised» column, opening: *«These are not books missing from a website — they are **books that exist, on a shelf in Istria, and cannot be read from anywhere else**.»* The research map repeated it: *«books that sit on a shelf in Istria and nowhere else»*.
rows.true:
**Pazin's column means «not digitised by Pazin». It says nothing about anybody else.**

Checked volume by volume against FamilySearch's films of the same parish, record type and years: **105 of the 154 are already photographed** — often inside one long reel that swallows several of Pazin's shelfmarks at once. Barban's *Births 1716–1750*, *1750–1781* and *1781–1816* are three Pazin volumes and **one FamilySearch film**.

**Forty-nine are left** — the ones where two catalogues agree nothing has been photographed. The page now leads with those, and they are the only ones worth a letter.

*Found by looking at the map's own panel.* Svetvinčenat's volume list showed «Births 1568–1588 ↗» and «Births 1568–1588 — not digitised anywhere» on consecutive lines, which cannot both be true. **The duplication I had been treating as a display problem was the archive telling me the claim was wrong.**

rows.what: «Every parish in Croatia whose registers are on film»
rows.said: The research map's standfirst, since it was built: *«Every parish in Croatia whose registers are on film, and how far this archive has got with each one.»*
rows.true:
**It is every parish in one collection.** *Croatia, Church Books, 1516–1994*, plus three sources added by hand. FamilySearch publishes **3,488 collections**, and Croatian places are scattered through the ones named for other countries — because **a town's registers are filed by whichever state kept them, under the name that state used**.

**Čakovec is filmed as «Csáktornya», in a Hungarian county, inside a collection named for Slovenia.** Five Croatian Istrian parishes are inside an Italian one. A second Croatian church-book collection exists for the Delnice deanery and browses by film number, so no place-based walk would ever find it.

The standfirst now says what the map actually is, and [a page lists what it cannot see](/elsewhere/).

*Found because David asked whether Croatian towns might be recorded in other countries' books.* They are, and the map had been quietly claiming otherwise for two days.

rows.what: The About page listed ten sources while the archive was using ninety-three
rows.said: A table headed **Sources**, hand-typed into the page: Pazin, istrianet, defranceski.com, Forebears, Acta Croatica, Antenati, FamilySearch, the Udine diocesan archive, Rijeka — **ten rows**, unchanged since the archive's first week.
rows.true:
**There are 83 sources in the register and 274 searches recorded against them.** The ten were the ones that existed when the page was written, and the list never caught up while ANNO, Hungaricana, Findmypast, Trove, Matricula, 23andMe, the Statue of Liberty database, the Arolsen Archives, Mémoire des Hommes, CEMLA and eighty others were added.

**The table is now driven by the source register itself**, grouped by kind, so it cannot fall behind again — and it points at [the search register](/searched/), which records every search including the ones that found nothing.

rows.what: The research map was in no menu at all
rows.said: Two days of work went into the research map, the collection walk, the undigitised list and the Antenati catalogue. **None of them was in the navigation.** The map could be reached only by a link inside another page.
rows.true:
**Five pages were orphaned** — the research map, «Croatia filed abroad», «Every collection walked», «The undigitised» and the Antenati registers. All five are now in the **Evidence** menu beside Parish Books.

*Found because David asked which menu the map was in.* It was in none, and the build's «nothing links to it» warning had been satisfied by a single in-page link each time — which is not the same as being findable.

rows.what: A backspace character in a regular expression hid every Italian birth and death register
rows.said: Mione's panel showed **one record type — Marriages**, and thirty-three volumes filed under «Other: titles this archive cannot classify». Twenty-three other Carnian and Istrian comuni said the same. The map could not draw a births or deaths timeline for **the parish this whole family comes out of**, and could not show that Mione's civil births stop in 1810 — a finding the archive had already published in words on [the Carnia page](/carnia/).
rows.true:
**«Nati» and «Morti» were unmatchable.** The patch of 15 September that taught the classifier its Hungarian words wrote the word boundaries into a **non-raw Python string**, so «\\b» was stored as an actual backspace character. The pattern became «nati⌫» and «morti⌫» — two alternatives that can never match anything, in a file where nothing looks wrong, because a terminal prints a backspace by moving the cursor.

**248 volumes across 24 places** were in «Other» because of it, sixteen of them already read. Mione now shows **Births 1806–1810, ALL READ**, Marriages and Deaths, each with 1807 named as a gap.

*Found because David asked whether the green on one Gračišće row meant the same as the green on the block around it.* It did not — that was a second bug, fixed the same hour — but checking the same thing on Mione and Ovaro is what turned this one up.

rows.what: No record-type heading on the map had been amber since the read ledger changed shape
rows.said: A heading was to turn **green when every volume of its kind had been read and amber when some had**. Green worked. Amber never appeared — a parish six volumes into eighteen looked exactly like one nobody had opened.
rows.true: The tint was keyed to the words **«N of M read»**, which is what the builder printed until the per-volume ledger arrived and changed the sentence to «6 read, 0 part read, 12 unopened». The test stopped matching and nothing said so. The ◐ mark beside the heading was right the whole time; the colour behind it was missing.

rows.what: Prato Carnico was on the map as Prato in Tuscany, and four Carnian villages were on it not at all
rows.said: **Prato** — sixty-two volumes of the Val Pesarina — sat on the map at **43.88 N, 11.10 E**: Prato in Tuscany, three hundred kilometres from Carnia. **Priola** sat in Piedmont. And **Pesariis (32 volumes), Colza (25), Pieria (10) and Osais (8)** had no dot at all, so their panels could not be opened and 75 volumes of the origin valley were invisible.
rows.true:
Three faults, one family of causes — a name looked up without a region.

**The four missing villages** are in GeoNames under compound names: *Osais-Pesariis*, *Tartinis-Colza*, *Pieria-Prato Carnico*. Only whole strings were indexed. The parts are indexed now, always below a place that carries the name on its own.

**Prato and Priola** are real names in more than one province, and the index keeps one row per name, ranked by population — so Tuscany's Prato, with 190,000 people, beat Prato Carnico's 1,065. A place catalogued only by a provider that works one valley is now resolved **inside that valley**: the Udine sources get a Friuli box, and the candidate in the box wins.

**«Prato» is written down as Prato Carnico** rather than left to a lookup to guess again. It is what the collection means — its own frazioni, Pesariis, Osais and Pieria, are listed beside it in the same collection.

*Found because David asked to check the rest of the Carnia panels after the «Nati» and «Morti» fix.* Six of the thirty were wrong or missing.

rows.what: Why a volume has no link was explained at the top of a panel a reader was reading the bottom of
rows.said: Gračišće's panel explained in its opening paragraph that Pazin publishes a register list and no images. Then it printed thirty-two titles that do not click, over seventeen hundred pixels, with the explanation long off the screen.
rows.true: The reason is now repeated as a **«No links»** row at the foot of the volume list, beside «Not digitised» and «No gaps» — where the eye is when the question occurs to it. *Asked twice by David, which is the measure of an answer in the wrong place.*

rows.what: Vodnjan was two places on the map, and the bigger one was not the family's
rows.said: Vodnjan stood on the map **twice** — one marker with nine volumes, and another a few pixels away with a hundred and thirty-three. **Umag** and **Motovun** were doubled the same way. A reader who clicked the nearer dot saw a ninth of the shelf.
rows.true:
Pazin's register list writes a town under both its names at once — **«Vodnjan / Dignano», «Umag / Umago», «Motovun / Montona»** — and the whole string was being keyed as a third place. Three towns and **383 volumes** were split off from themselves.

The town is the first name now and the second is filed as what it is *also written as*, which is a thing this panel already knew how to say. Vodnjan is one marker with **142 volumes** — 41 births from 1559, 44 marriages, 41 deaths, two real gaps named, and fifteen volumes that exist on paper and nowhere else.

rows.what: Ledenice was in the Czech Republic and Ragusa was in Sicily
rows.said: **Ledenice** — where **Anton Defranceschi was born in 1890** — was pinned at 48.93 N, 14.62 E: **Ledenice in South Bohemia**, eight hundred kilometres from the Vinodol. **Ragusa**, which is what every Venetian document calls Dubrovnik, was pinned in **Sicily**.
rows.true:
The gazetteer keeps the most populous bearer of a name, which is right almost always and wrong exactly here: Czech Ledenice has 2,000 people to the Vinodol village's 164, and Ragusa in Sicily has 69,000. **Population cannot tell a namesake from a home town.**

Both are now forced to the country the archive means, written down in the builder with the reason beside them rather than left to a count of inhabitants. Ledenice is at 45.14, 14.84; Ragusa resolves to Dubrovnik.

*Found while checking the Istrian panels after the Carnia ones.*

rows.what: Ragusa and Dubrovnik were two pins on the same ground, and the Dubrovnik city parish was labelled Ragusa
rows.said: **Ragusa** and **Dubrovnik** stood as two markers forty-five metres apart, four people and twenty-four volumes divided between them. Worse, the parish **Dubrovnik-Grad** — the city parish itself — carried the display name **«Ragusa»**, left behind by a hand-checked entry in an old place harvest.
rows.true:
One pin, four people, 24 volumes, and *Ragusa* among the names it is also written under.

The merge is made on a **written-down identity, never on proximity**: places.json already records what the other empires called each of these towns — Gallignana for Gračišće, Pisino and Mitterburg for Pazin, Dignano for Vodnjan, Ragusa for Dubrovnik — **forty-nine of them, curated by hand.** That table is now what folds two names into one pin, and the distance test still has to agree. *Gologorica and Gračišće are 2.4 km apart and stay two places, which is the rule this had to be built around.*

One more thing the merge exposed: a folded pin was taking only its own shelf, so Ragusa's twenty-one volumes vanished at the moment Ragusa became Dubrovnik. A merged pin now gathers the volumes of every name it swallowed.

rows.what: «A Puerto Rican cluster of the name» — it is the name without its particle
rows.said: The Findmypast sweep was published with a finding headed **«A Puerto Rican cluster of the name»** — fifty-two records across eleven towns, offered as a lead on the surname this archive is built on.
rows.true:
**Every one of the fifty-two is a woman**, and reading the names in Spanish says why. *Filomena Franceschi Dávila de Padilla. Carmen Callejo y Ferrer de Franceschi.* **«de» is the marital particle there, not the Italian nobiliary one.** A woman who marries a Franceschi is indexed *de Franceschi*; the men of the family are filed under plain **Franceschi** and a search for «de Franceschi» never sees them.

The cluster is real. It is a **Franceschi** family, seen through a keyhole, and the surname in it is not this archive's surname. Corrected on the page in place, with what the right search would be.

*Found within the hour, while building the map layer from the same 644 records — the place data made the pattern visible in a way the summary count never could.*

rows.what: Six more parishes in the wrong country, found by a test instead of by eye
rows.said: Carnia and Istria were checked because David asked about a panel, and nine places came back wrong. **Nobody had looked at the other twelve hundred.**
rows.true:
A script now applies the two tests the builders already had. **A place catalogued only by a provider that works one region cannot be outside that region**, and **a place whose own name carries a country cannot be in a different one.** It found six more.

**Senja, Sv. Juraj** — the Senj deanery's coastal parish, eight kilometres from the town this family's grandmother was born in — was **outside Belgrade**. **Sv. Jakov-Šiljevica**, which is the old name of Jadranovo four kilometres from [Crikvenica](/crikvenica-house/), was **in Šumadija**. **Klasnić** of the Banovina was in Šumadija too. **Krug** was in **Lower Austria**. And **Grad** and **Tišina**, both Prekmurje parishes, were in **Dalmatia**.

Three things were wrong underneath them. The region box existed only for the two Udine providers and now covers all seven. **«Sv.» was being stripped and never expanded** — GeoNames writes the patron out in full, so *Sveti Jakov Šiljevica* and *Sv. Jakov-Šiljevica* never met. And **this builder had never read data/gazetteer.json at all**, which is where a coordinate checked by hand lives with its reason beside it, so a hand fix could not reach the research map however carefully it was written.

The audit now reports **zero**. It is [scripts/place-audit.py], it changes nothing itself, and it should be run whenever a place is added.

rows.what: Maria Defranceschi of Gologorica was in this archive twice
rows.said: Two roster rows, **born 1786** and **born 1789**, dying in the same year at the same parish, under two MyHeritage identifiers — 4509439 and 4510756.
rows.true:
**One woman.** [The reconciliation against the live tree](/live-tree/) returned the pair **mirrored**: our 1786 against the tree's 1789 and our 1789 against the tree's 1786, which is the shape a duplicate makes when both sides hold it. Merged, with both identifiers kept on the surviving row.

**The birth year is still not settled.** 1786 is kept because it is the row that carries the parish, and the Gologorica baptisms will decide between them.

*Petrus Defranceschi came back mirrored in the same pass and has NOT been merged*: his two rows disagree on the parish — a Petrus of Rovinj resting on a burial register with an ark, against a Petrus of Gologorica resting on the 2018 family file — and a burial entry outranks a tree entry. Both now carry a note saying so.

rows.what: An infant and an eighty-year-old were reported as the same person disagreeing about a date
rows.said: [The reconciliation](/live-tree/) published **fourteen** anchored disagreements this morning, the first of them **Antonius Defranceschi — tree 1814–1893, archive 1893–1893**.
rows.true:
**They are two people.** Antonius of Gologorica died in 1893 aged seventy-nine. The other Antonius was **buried at Pula as an infant in 1893** — born and buried in the same year, which is why his row reads 1893–1893. **Twenty of this archive's burial rows look like that**, because a burial register of a child gives both dates at once.

The anchor test was written to stop exactly this: two people of one name and no shared year are two people. **It did not occur to it that two people can share one year and still be an infant and an old man.** The test now refuses any pair where one life is five years or less and the other thirty or more. Three rows went with it — Antonius, a *Giovanni* aged three against a *Giovanni* of seventy, and a *Maria* who died in infancy against a Maria who lived to forty-seven.

**Fourteen becomes twelve, and the twelve are then sorted by what kind of disagreement they are** — seven that are a year of age-arithmetic, two that are too large for it, and three where the death year itself is disputed. Only the last kind needs a register.

*Found while working the fourteen one by one, which is what the work-list row asked for.*

rows.what: «668 people the archive has never heard of» — it was never 668, and the first two answers were both wrong
rows.said: The reconciliation published **668 people only in the tree**, offered as *«where the next month of work is»*.
rows.true:
**Twice wrong, and the second time on this very page.**

**First**: 486 of them are inside David's own placeholder pens — twenty-three country folders with town folders beneath, under a node he labelled *«for Investigation (not real)»*. He had already tested and parked them. Counting that as untouched work was backwards.

**Then the remainder was announced as 113, and that was wrong too.** The join compared the **whole set** of given names, and the live tree stacks every variant it has ever seen into one string: *«Johannes Giovanni Gian Battista de Franceschi»* against this archive's *«Giovanni Defranceschi»* is four names against one, so **the top of David's own male line was reported as a stranger** — and this page said of him, in as many words, *«that is not a namesake to be tested, it is a hole»*. He is [in the roster and in the spine](/direct-line/), born 1750 at Gologorica and dead 1829, exactly as the tree has him.

**The test is now: the same set of given names, or one name in common and a year in common.** It is in the builder rather than in prose, so the page cannot drift from it again. **The honest figure is 84.** They stand at Ližnjan, Crikvenica, Gračišće, Gologorica, Brooklyn, and two beside Pfullingen.

rows.what: «Trove's search needs a free registered key» — it does not
rows.said: That Australian newspapers at **Trove** could only be searched with *«a free registered key — a job for a person with an account»*, and the Broken Hill graves were therefore left for a human being.
rows.true:
**The key is for the API. The website searches without one, and always has.** Trove was searched from a browser on 17 September on four spellings across every digitised gazette, and it answered in an afternoon: [the day Zdravko and Ruža became Australians](/pfullingen/#gazette), the son who took the oath five months before them in another state, and one line for Broken Hill — *«DeFranceschi Bros, 716 Chappie Lane»*, in the New South Wales Government Gazette of 17 June 1966.

**The cost of the mistake was two months.** A job written down as needing a person with an account is a job that does not get done, and this one needed nothing but a browser.

rows.what: «The per-record output was never written to disk» — it was, and it had been sitting in the repository for two days
rows.said: That the forty burials with no parish *«cannot be placed from anything in this repository»*, because the Istrian sweep's per-record output — ark by ark — **was never written to disk**, and that re-harvesting forty personas from FamilySearch was «half a day».
rows.true:
**`data/parish-by-record-2026-09.txt` has been in the repository since 8 September**: ninety-three parishes, and under each of them the 952 persona ids the sweep read there. Only the ninety-three-row summary was ever published, so the file went quiet, and a row was then written asserting it did not exist.

**All thirty-six placed in an afternoon with no search at all** — twenty-five on the id the sweep already held, eleven on its twin. The lesson is not about FamilySearch. **A file that nothing links to is a file the archive will shortly claim it never had.**

rows.what: Ninety-two people were told nothing had been read about them, on pages printing what had been read about them
rows.said: Person pages carried, in as many words, *«This person has no recorded year»*, *«born about 1749 — estimated, not recorded»*, and *«No family is drawn for this name, and no record stands behind it… the name reached this project through a chart, a narrative source or the family tree»*.
rows.true:
**For ninety-two of them that was false, and the evidence was in this repository the whole time.**

**Nine of Valentino's children.** On 6 September the Liber Baptizatorum of Fiume was read and the fourteen children of Valentino Defranceschi were written to `site/src/data/valentino.json`. **No build script and no page ever read that file** — for eleven days. Five of the children had pages estimating a birth «about 1749» over the top of an exact baptism date sitting on disk; **four had no page at all**, and their baptisms exist in no index anywhere, so this archive was the only place they survived. The file's fault was that it had **no key to a person**: it writes *«Josepha Catharina»* where the archive has *«Josepham Catharinam Defranceschi»*, the accusative the clerk used, and no name match was ever going to join those.

**And eighty-three more, for a different reason.** The «no record stands behind it» banner tested only whether a person had a household chart or a FamilySearch index strip. It never looked at their **records**. So **Cesare De Franceschi** was told no record stood behind his name two sections above his own headstone — *«Headstone – 30 Jan 2005 · Gungahlin Cemetery and Crematorium»* — and eighty-two others like him.

**Every gate was green while this was true**: links, anchors, living people, the work list, the errand ledger. All of them look at what IS on the page. **None looked from the evidence back to the person.** [One does now](/method/), and it refuses the build.
rows.how: `scripts/check-evidence.py`, wired into `npm run build` as `check:evidence`. It reads the rendered site, not the data, because the failure it guards against happens between the two. Verified by reintroducing both bugs: the first fails 9, the second 88, each exits 1.

rows.what: Four spellings on «Say Your Name» were filed as a language's form of a name, and three of them are a clerk's mistake
rows.said: That **Vitnio** and **Valentio** are Italian forms of *Vittorio* and *Valentino*, that **Antonÿ** is an English form of *Antonio*, and that **Felix** and **Srećko** are Italian forms of *Felice*.
rows.true:
**Three of those are not forms of a name at all, they are one hand getting it wrong once.** *Vitnio* is Vitorio with the r read as an n, on an infant's burial at Svetvinčenat in 1815. *Valentio* is Valentino with the n dropped, on one of his own children's entries while three others spell him properly. *Antonÿ* is the clerk's ligature for the double i of the genitive *Antonii* — a letterform, not an English spelling.

And **Felix is the Latin form, Srećko the Croatian one**; only *Felice* is Italian.

The distinction is not pedantry. **A language form can be looked up; a slip can only be recognised**, and filing the two together hid the harder kind. There is now [a cited list of the slips](/your-name/#slips) — ten of them, four belonging to one man — and the search box answers to them, so a reader holding an Arolsen card that says **JVAN** can type what is in front of them.

rows.what: «Say Your Name» said it was built from the registers and not from a dictionary. A third of it was a dictionary
rows.said: «**Every name below was reconciled by hand from the forms that actually appear in these registers — not from a dictionary.**»
rows.true:
**130 of the 415 forms on the page — thirty-one per cent — appeared in no record this archive holds.** The Croatian column was the worst of them: **31 of its 48 forms** had never been seen written down here. And dozens sat under the wrong language outright. *Antal* and *Ilona* are **Hungarian** and were filed as Italian. So were *Božo*, *Tomislav*, *Jerolim*, *Pasko*, *Terezija*, *Karlo* and a dozen more **Croatian** forms, and *Steven*, *Jasper*, *Noel*, *Dominic* and *Benedict*, which are **English**. *Bartholomaeus* was filed as German and is Latin; *Srećko* as Italian and is Croatian.

**And there was no Hungarian column at all** — in an archive whose own place-strings read *«Vitipolis, Modrus-Fiume, **Magyarország**»*, for a family whose Fiume parish was in the Kingdom of Hungary and whose registers went over to Hungarian in 1895. Sixteen Hungarian forms were already sitting in the records unrecognised.

**Deleting the dictionary forms would have been the wrong fix.** A form nobody here has met is still the right thing to type into a Hungarian or a German index tomorrow. So the table now keeps both kinds and **says which is which** — 419 of 645 cells attested in a record, 226 marked as lookup aids — across **seven** columns and **73** names, twelve of them new (Giorgio, Giulio, Elisabetta, Angela, Sebastiano, Bernardo, Leonardo, Pasquale, Mario, Marta, Mattea, Oliva), every one of which occurs in these records and had no row.

Two wrong equivalences went with it: **Marta is Martha, not a form of Margarita**, and it has its own row now; **Agneza is Agnes, not Agata**, and it is gone, because this archive has never met it.
rows.how: `scripts/name-forms-audit.py`, wired into `npm run build` as `check:names`. It looks every form up in the roster, the register, the households, the burials, the headstones and the four FamilySearch harvests, and refuses the build if a form stored as attested is in no record. Verified by marking *Gergely* and *Gregor* attested: exits 1 and names both.

rows.what: «Somebody should photograph that lintel» — five photographs of it were in this archive already
rows.said: «**Somebody should photograph that lintel.** It has been on this archive's list of things to look for since the beginning, and it has just gone from a guess to a target.»
rows.true:
**The family photographed it in the field, and the pictures have been on the [gallery](/gallery/) ever since.** *The arms, and the Madonna beneath them* — the oval cartouche in high relief with its mantling and plumed helm, on the façade at Gologorica. *The builder's tablet, on the front of the house.* *The blazon, cut in stone on the tomb.* *The same arms, worn almost away*, on an older stone in the same ground. And the house itself from the lane.

The page that argues the carving exists was the one page not showing it. **They are on it now.**

**What is still genuinely wanted is narrower and worth stating exactly**, because the retraction should not swallow the real gap: every frame the archive holds was taken in flat light from wherever a person could stand, and **none of them settles the fruit** — which is the whole argument, Carlo's pomegranate against the cousins' turnip. [The shot list](/photograph-these/) has been asking all along for the cartouche straight on, filling the frame, in raking light.
rows.how: Found by [David](/about/), reading the page. The same fault as the [valentino.json](/corrections/) one earlier the same day and the [Trove key](/corrections/) one before it: the archive holding a thing and the page saying it does not.

rows.what: «The normaliser behind the household pages carries 645 recorded forms» — no normaliser read the table at all
rows.said: That the given-name table was the instrument behind the joins: «**The normaliser behind the household pages now carries 73 canonical names across 645 recorded forms**, in Latin, Italian, Venetian, Croatian, German and English.»
rows.true:
**Nothing read it.** `givennames.json` was imported by two pages that display it and by nothing else — not by `build-dossiers.py`, not by `lib/people.js`, not by any script that joins a record to a person. **Both** normalisers in this archive fold the *surname* and stop:

· `_nm()` lowercases, strips diacritics and maps *defranceschi* → *de franceschi*.
· `norm()` in `lib/people.js` does the same.

Neither touches a given name. So **Josephus, Giuseppe and Josip were three strangers** to every join on this site, and the page reconciling them said it was already fixed.

**327 of the 1,122 person pages are in a group of this kind** — 98 groups. *Ivan Defranceski*, *Ivan de Franceschi*, *Joannem Defranceschi*, *Joannes Defranceschi*, *Giovanni Defranceschi*, *Giovanni de Franceschi* and *Zuane De Franceschi* are seven pages.

**The fix is a cross-reference, not a merge.** Identity here is by name on purpose, and collapsing Ivan into Giovanni by machine is the join this archive spends its time refusing. Each page now names the others and says plainly that none of them is claimed to be the same person.
rows.how: Found by David asking whether the archive actually *searches* with these forms. It does not do that either — see the work list.

rows.what: «Not one of them is this family» — filed forty-nine records of the name as nothing, in an archive that exists for the name
rows.said: That the first search of The National Archives at Kew found **«nothing of this family»**, outcome **«nothing»**. And, at the top of the front page, that this is *«**A family** written down under eight sovereigns»*.
rows.true:
**This site has never been about one family and the site says so itself**, two screens below that sentence: *«There is no single Defranceschi family. Six families carry the name and this archive follows all six.»* The front page contradicted its own card, and a Kew search written by that wrong measure threw away everything it found.

**Seven of those records are the name in Britain and belong here**: a *Franceschi* in the State Papers for Venice in **1677**; **Mark Franceschi**, master of the *Amabile*, taken as prize and appealed at Minorca in **1805**; three Great War medal cards for **Lorenzo, Ernest and William C. Franceschi**; and **Lorenzo Franceschi** of London, from Italy, naturalised 4 April 1934, wife Agnes Elizabeth. Eleven more are **Franceschin-** — the diminutive, a different surname — and are filed as adjacent rather than discarded.

**Britain had no entry on [where the name went](/diaspora/#britain)** despite a Cardiff marriage of 1876, a Cardiff recital of 1896 and a barque out of the Bute Docks in 1877 all sitting in these pages. It has one now.

**The lesson is about scope, not about Kew.** *«Is this our bloodline?»* is the wrong question to ask of a record while collecting; it is the right question only when claiming. Collect on the name, claim on the evidence — and this archive had the two the wrong way round for an afternoon.
rows.how: Caught by David, in one sentence: «this site was never for 1 family, its always been for the defranceski name and its different lines / origins.»

rows.what: «Franceschini» was listed among the eleven forms of this name. It is a different surname
rows.said: The table of forms carried **Franceschini** as one of them — *«Trentino, Friuli, Tuscany — and four people in this archive»* — beside De Franceschi, Defranceschi and Defranceski.
rows.true:
**De Franceschi is a genitive plural — «of the Franceschi». Franceschini is a diminutive of Francesco, formed separately and meaning something else.** They meet in an index and nowhere else.

The distinction matters more here than it would elsewhere, because **this archive studies a name rather than a family** and therefore collects on the name. That makes the edge of the name load-bearing: everything inside it counts, so everything outside it has to be marked. **Thirty-six pages here carry an adjacent surname**, most swept up by an Austrian harvest.

**They keep their pages and they are now banded** — deleting a person because a ruling went against their surname would be its own dishonesty, and the next researcher needs to see they were looked at and set aside. [Where the name stops](/name/#scope) is written down, with the thirteen spellings that are this name and the five that only collide with it.
rows.how: Ruled by David, 17 September 2026, on a question this archive put to him.

rows.what: The direct line put Anton Rudolf's birth at Crikvenica in one generation and at Klenovica in the next
rows.said: Generation four: *«He is the generation that leaves Istria for the Kvarner coast: **his son is born at Crikvenica in 1890**.»*
rows.true:
**Generation five, on the same page, cites the record**: *«Entry 9 of the **Klenovica** baptisms for 1890: Anton Rudolf, legitimate, son of «Josip Defranceschi i žena Ana Kalanj rodjena», at house 22.»* Klenovica is in the Vinodol below Novi, not at Crikvenica, and the register is the better witness than the summary above it.

**It is not a quibble about ten kilometres — it decides which parish to search.** The family's Kvarner records begin at **Klenovica** and the bride, **Anna Kalanj**, was baptised at **Ledenice** — «entry 2 of 1864, daughter of Josephus Kalanj and Rosalia née Perković, at Rijenovica house 22». Croatian custom marries in the bride's parish, so the marriage this archive is looking for should be sought at Ledenice first and Crikvenica second.
rows.how: Found while planning the search of the Crikvenica marriage film — the two generations were read side by side for the first time.

rows.what: The direct line carried Ivan's birth as «24 or 25 June» and would not choose
rows.said: Generation six: *«born **24 or 25 June 1925**»* — two dates printed side by side because two documents disagreed and the archive would not pick one.
rows.true:
**25 June 1925.** David ruled it on 17 September 2026. The disagreement is real and its source is now clear: the **1947 Pfullingen list of foreigners** says 24 June, his own **Allgemeine Ortskrankenkasse** card says 25 June, and Arolsen's indexers preserved both — the online archive carries him **four times**, as *Iwan* (24.06), *JVAN* (25.06), *IWAN* (25.06) and *JWAN* (24.06), one record per spelling per date.

**The card is the better witness.** It was made from him, on entering work, rather than compiled about him from a municipal roll two years after the war. His death is not in dispute: **30 October 1995**, and the gravestone at Senj reads IVAN DEFRANČESKI, 1925–1995.
rows.how: Given by David on 17 September 2026, the same hour the Arolsen inquiry went in citing all four records.

rows.what: Hedviga's birthday was printed two ways on two pages, and the archive had declined to choose
rows.said: The Senj line and [the Crikvenica house](/crikvenica-house/) both gave *«born at Senj on **8 March 1926**»*, while [1948](/1948/) set out the clash and concluded: *«This archive does not know which is right and **will not pick the one it likes**.»*
rows.true:
**3 August 1926.** The two dates are the same numbers in the wrong order — 8/3 against 3/8 — a European date meeting an English-speaking clerk. But they are not two page-texts of equal weight: **3 August comes from a certified extract of the Senj birth register**, the one attached to her son's 1951 birth entry and translated for the Supreme Court of South Africa. David's own tree gives 3 August too. A certified register extract beats a date carried in prose.

**The roster had already moved and the narrative pages had not** — the same fault this archive keeps finding in itself: a ruling that reaches one file and not the rest.
rows.how: Found while checking a different date on the same couple. David confirmed on 17 September 2026 that **her death on 30 October 2001, six years to the day after Ivan died at Senj, is a genuine coincidence** — both dates stand, and the family has always talked of it as a bit spooky. The birthday clash turned up in the course of confirming it. **Confirmed by David the same day, independently of the extract**: *«hedvigas birthday was in august 3»*. So this one is closed on three witnesses that agree — the certified register extract, the live tree, and the family. It does not need opening again.

rows.what: The scope list counted «Franceschich» as this name, and it is a different surname
rows.said: Thirteen spellings were declared in scope, among them **Franceschich**, and [the drift chart](/name/) drew it as a branch of *De Franceschi* from 1850 with the note *«Slavic -ić written the Austrian way»* — that is, *Franceschi* plus a Slavic suffix.
rows.true:
**It is the reverse, and the name is somebody else's.** *Franceschich* is the Italianised spelling of **Frančić**, the Croatian patronymic of *Franjo* — Francis's son — formed from the forename directly, exactly as *Franceschini* and the other diminutives are. It converges in spelling with this surname and shares nothing else.

**Twelve spellings are now in scope; six are adjacent.** The row has been taken off the drift chart as well as the list, because a chart of how *this* surname branches cannot draw a branch that is not it.

**Nobody is displaced.** No person in this archive carried the spelling — it was a claim about the language, not about a household.
rows.how: **Found by the Crikvenica marriage film, which is what a complete reading is for.** Two witnesses spelled **Franić / Frančić** appear in the 1888 marriages, at entries 6 and 18. Under the old list they were either two hits or an error on the list, and it could not be both. **David ruled on 20 September 2026: *«frančić is adjacent, take franceschich off the list»*** — so the seven-year negative for 1883–1889 stands unqualified, and the list loses a spelling it should never have had.

rows.what: Marija Stjepanka was baptised at Ledenice, not Crikvenica — and the entry gives the family's address
rows.said: Marija Stjepanka, the second child of Josip Defranceschi and Ana Kalanj, was recorded as **«8 December 1892 · Crikvenica»**, in the list of children born at the Crikvenica house.
rows.true:
**She was born on 8 December 1892 — that part is right — but she was baptised on 22 December at LEDENICE, and her parents were living at Klenovica.**

The entry is **Ledenice baptisms, page 166, no. 83**: *«Godine 1892, Prosinca 8 / 22 — **Marija Stjepanka** — zakonita — **Josip Defranceschi, klesar, i žena Ana Kalanj rodjena** — R.k. — mjesto obitavanja i kućni broj: **Klenovica kbroj 28, na stan**»*. A small note above the child's name reads **«u Crkvenici»**.

**Three things follow.** The father is called **klesar — a stonecutter** — in 1892, the trade his own father Antonius held at Gračišće in 1863. The family's address is **Klenovica house 28, «na stan» — in lodgings** — not the Kalanj house at no. 22 but a rented room a few doors from it. And **the household was still inside the Ledenice parish at the end of 1892**, not yet at Crikvenica: the move must fall between December 1892 and November 1894, when Ivan is born at Crikvenica.

*Found by querying the FamilySearch index for the surname directly and then reading the register page.*
